articles.title: Currículo criativo ajuda a driblar a IA? Veja quando inovar atrapalha | G1
articles.standfirst: Especialistas explicam quando formatos criativos podem destacar o candidato e em quais situações inovação, currículo impresso ou abordagens fora do padrão podem atrapalhar a seleção.
articles.summary: Especialistas explicam quando formatos criativos podem destacar o candidato e em quais situações inovação ou abordagens fora do padrão podem atrapalhar a seleção.
articles.body:
O designer australiano Felix Toohey cria currículos criativos e personalizados para cada empresa, transformando a candidatura em objetos e experiências inusitadas para chamar a atenção dos recrutadores. — Foto: Reprodução/Redes Sociais

Enquanto muitos candidatos apostam em portfólios elaborados, cartas de apresentação personalizadas ou mensagens no LinkedIn para chamar a atenção dos recrutadores, o designer australiano Felix Toohey decidiu seguir um caminho bem diferente: transformar o próprio currículo em uma experiência física e impossível de ignorar.

Morador de Melbourne, Toohey entrega pessoalmente os currículos às empresas onde sonha trabalhar . Mas vai além. Em vez de distribuir documentos convencionais, ele cria uma apresentação diferente para cada empresa e transforma o currículo em objetos e experiências pensados para seus potenciais empregadores.

No Instagram, ele compartilha algumas das criações com seus seguidores. Em uma das criações mais conhecidas, o currículo foi apresentado em uma bandeja de café . Copos de papel personalizados traziam, em formato de “latte art”, os títulos de cada seção, como formação acadêmica e experiência profissional.

As criações fazem parte da série "Ghosting Busters" (em tradução livre, "caçadores de ghosting"), projeto em que Toohey desenvolve currículos cada vez mais excêntricos para se destacar em um mercado de trabalho competitivo.

Apesar da repercussão, a estratégia ainda não resultou em uma vaga fixa . O projeto, no entanto, abriu outras portas. A Canva, por exemplo, fez uma parceria com o designer para produzir um vídeo patrocinado inspirado na série "Ghosting Busters".

🤔 Mas, trazendo a discussão para a realidade do mercado de trabalho brasileiro, até que ponto um currículo inovador ajuda a driblar o avanço da inteligência artificial nos processos seletivos? E ainda vale imprimir o documento e entregá-lo pessoalmente?

Segundo especialistas ouvidos pelo g1 , a resposta depende de fatores como o tipo de vaga, a área de atuação e a forma como as empresas utilizam ferramentas de inteligência artificial na seleção.

Para Maria Paula Oliveira, diretora de recursos humanos da LG lugar de Gente, um currículo criativo pode chamar a atenção do recrutador, mas não garante, por si só, uma contratação .

A originalidade funciona como uma espécie de cartão de visitas e pode despertar curiosidade na primeira análise. A decisão, porém, continua baseada principalmente na combinação entre qualificações, competências e experiência profissional.

Na avaliação da especialista, existe uma linha tênue entre chamar atenção e criar obstáculos para a própria candidatura . Formatos muito complexos, informações difíceis de localizar ou ações consideradas invasivas podem gerar uma impressão negativa.

A especialista afirma que a criatividade tende a funcionar melhor em profissões nas quais a apresentação visual já faz parte do trabalho , como marketing, publicidade, design, criação de conteúdo, moda, arquitetura e comunicação.

Já em setores como jurídico, financeiro e técnico, a recomendação é priorizar a organização das informações, a clareza e os resultados alcançados.

Outro ponto importante é que personalizar o documento não significa criar um layout diferente para cada empresa, mas destacar experiências e competências relacionadas aos requisitos da posição . Essa adaptação também pode facilitar a análise por sistemas de recrutamento que utilizam inteligência artificial.

Currículos com dados inseridos em gráficos, imagens ou elementos visuais muito complexos podem ter parte das informações ignorada durante a triagem automatizada. Com isso, experiências relevantes podem deixar de ser identificadas.

Por isso, quem aposta em uma apresentação diferenciada deve manter também uma versão convencional do currículo , especialmente para inscrições feitas por plataformas digitais.

A especialista também recomenda calibrar o grau de ousadia de acordo com a empresa . “A mesma ideia pode ser lida como iniciativa numa empresa e como desconexão de contexto em outra”, afirma.

Para quem deseja se destacar sem correr o risco de parecer interessado apenas em repercussão, a executiva recomenda que qualquer iniciativa diferenciada esteja diretamente relacionada às competências exigidas pela vaga.

“No caso de Felix Toohey, o currículo criativo funciona também como portfólio. A criatividade faz sentido porque demonstra, na prática, as habilidades que ele utiliza no trabalho. Quando não existe essa conexão, a estratégia pode gerar mais ruído do que valor”, conclui.

Para Patricia Suzuki, diretora de RH da Redarbor Brasil, entregar o currículo pessoalmente perdeu espaço com a digitalização dos processos seletivos.

Hoje, muitas empresas recebem e fazem a triagem das candidaturas por meio de sites. Por isso, quando a companhia estabelece um canal oficial, aparecer pessoalmente não substitui a candidatura digital.

Em empresas menores ou estabelecimentos comerciais, uma abordagem presencial educada e adequada ao contexto ainda pode ajudar a criar contato .

Patricia também recomenda adaptar o currículo à vaga, ajustando o título, o resumo profissional, as experiências e as competências de acordo com o que a empresa procura.

A orientação vale especialmente para processos digitais, nos quais sistemas automatizados podem fazer a primeira análise.

“O candidato pode ter uma apresentação visual diferenciada, mas deve garantir que cargo, experiências, formação, competências e demais informações relevantes estejam em texto claro”, diz.

A diretora alerta ainda para o risco de transformar a candidatura em uma tentativa de viralização . Excesso de elementos visuais, humor inadequado, abordagens desconectadas da vaga ou formatos que priorizam a surpresa em detrimento da clareza podem prejudicar a impressão causada no recrutador.

“O currículo não deve parecer mais preocupado em impressionar do que em comunicar o perfil profissional”, afirma.

Independentemente do formato, Patricia diz que o documento precisa permitir que o recrutador encontre rapidamente informações básicas , como contato profissional, área de interesse, experiências, formação e competências relevantes. Idiomas, certificações, cursos e portfólio também podem ser incluídos quando fizerem sentido para a vaga.

“O objetivo não deve ser fazer o recrutador lembrar do candidato pela excentricidade, mas pela combinação entre relevância, clareza e capacidade de demonstrar valor para aquela oportunidade”, completa.

Quer inovar no currículo? Veja o que fazer e o que evitar

Especialistas ouvidas pelo g1 dão algumas recomendações para quem deseja se destacar nos processos seletivos sem comprometer a análise do currículo.

➡️ Comece pela vaga, não pela ideia : antes de pensar em um formato criativo, entenda o que a empresa procura e quais competências são importantes para a posição.

✍🏽 Adapte o conteúdo à vaga : personalize o currículo destacando experiências, competências e resultados que tenham relação direta com os requisitos da vaga.

✅ Priorize a clareza : contato, experiência profissional, formação acadêmica e competências devem estar organizados de forma simples e fácil de localizar. Se o design dificultar a leitura, a estratégia pode ter efeito contrário.

🧐 Use a criatividade para demonstrar uma habilidade : um designer pode explorar recursos visuais; um profissional de comunicação pode apostar em uma narrativa diferenciada. A inovação funciona melhor quando comprova uma competência relevante para a função.

🚫 Considere a área e a cultura da empresa : formatos criativos costumam funcionar melhor em áreas como design, publicidade, marketing, comunicação e audiovisual. Além disso, uma iniciativa que faz sentido em uma startup pode não ter o mesmo efeito em uma empresa mais tradicional.

💻 Tenha uma versão tradicional para candidaturas digitais : mesmo que opte por um modelo criativo, mantenha uma versão convencional para inscrições feitas em plataformas de recrutamento e sites de carreira.

😥 Não confunda criatividade com excentricidade : excesso de elementos visuais, humor inadequado, informações difíceis de encontrar ou abordagens invasivas podem fazer o candidato ser lembrado pelo motivo errado.

articles.title: Por que você nunca realmente supera a época de ensino médio? | G1
articles.standfirst: A popularidade, uma das principais obsessões da adolescência, parece ficar gravada em nossa consciência por décadas depois que deixamos a escola.
articles.summary: A popularidade, uma das principais obsessões da adolescência, parece ficar gravada em nossa consciência por décadas depois que deixamos a escola.
articles.body:
Por que você nunca realmente supera a época de ensino médio: 'São lembranças que voltam o tempo todo' — Foto: Emmanuel Lafont/BBC

A popularidade, uma das principais obsessões da adolescência, parece ficar gravada em nossa consciência por décadas depois que deixamos a escola.

Antes de virar amiga de Georgia*, eu tinha medo dela.

Um episódio ficou na minha memória. Nós tínhamos 14 anos, e minha melhor amiga na época estava dando uma festa, daquelas que acontecem em um salão de igreja alugado e todos os alunos da série comparecem. Mas havia um grupo de pessoas que minha amiga tinha esquecido de convidar.

Georgia e seu grupo vieram em nossa direção pelo pátio, enquanto as pessoas ao redor se viravam para olhar. Ela era uma assustadora combinação de bronzeamento artificial, extensões de cabelo descolorido e roupas esportivas fluorescentes. O que alguém como ela poderia querer com gente como nós?

"Estamos convidadas para a sua festa, né?", exigiu Georgia à minha amiga. "Sim, claro", minha amiga conseguiu responder, gaguejando. Satisfeita, Georgia deu meia-volta e saiu marchando.

Outra garota que estava por perto murmurou: "Você não precisa convidá-las se não quiser". Mas todas nós sabíamos que sim, ela precisava.

Provavelmente você também tem lembranças parecidas do ensino médio e da parte cruel das disputas políticas da escola. Talvez tenha lembranças de uma Georgia na sua vida, uma garota popular que conseguia provocar medo com um simples olhar. Talvez você mesmo tenha sido uma Georgia.

Seja como for, você provavelmente tem memórias marcantes dessa época. Depois de conversar com centenas de pessoas sobre suas experiências no ensino médio, Mitch Prinstein, professor de psicologia da Universidade da Carolina do Norte em Chapel Hill, nos Estados Unidos, descobriu que as lembranças das pessoas que um dia dominaram os corredores da escola (as garotas populares, os 'príncipes' das festas, os atletas estrelas) eram extraordinariamente fortes.

Mesmo décadas depois de deixar a escola, a maioria das pessoas consegue se lembrar sem esforço do nome do aluno mais popular de seu ano. Com mais facilidade, inclusive, do que dos nomes de professores e de outros colegas de classe, escreveu Prinstein em seu livro de 2017 Popular: The Power of Likability in a Status-Obsessed World (Popular: o poder de ser gostado em um mundo obcecado por status, em tradução livre).

E não são apenas as lembranças que permanecem. Podemos imaginar que a hierarquia do ensino médio se torna irrelevante depois que atravessamos os portões da escola pela última vez. Mas, ao que parece, ela pode continuar exercendo em nós um domínio estranho e persistente.

Pesquisas mostram que o quanto éramos populares e queridos na adolescência pode influenciar nossas vidas por muitos anos, afetando desde a maneira como interpretamos nossas interações sociais até a qualidade de nossos relacionamentos amorosos, nossa satisfação com a vida e até mesmo nossa saúde.

Foi o psicólogo americano John Coie quem mudou a maneira como os pesquisadores pensavam na popularidade.

Seus estudos, hoje considerados fundamentais, realizados no início dos anos 1980, começaram com duas perguntas simples feitas a crianças em idade escolar sobre seus colegas:

De quem você mais gosta? De quem você menos gosta?

Lendo as respostas de caligrafia infantil em centenas de pedaços de papel, Coie identificou novos insights sobre o comportamento social humano.

Uma possível suposição é que algumas crianças seriam, de modo geral, mais queridas pelos colegas, enquanto outras seriam mais rejeitadas.

Mas Coie e os outros pesquisadores também perceberam algo diferente. Algumas crianças eram ao mesmo tempo queridas e rejeitadas por alunos diferentes; enquanto outras não eram nem queridas nem rejeitadas.

Ou seja, alguns eram mencionados muitas vezes pelos colegas, sendo altamente visíveis, quase como pequenas celebridades. E outros mal apareciam nas respostas.

Coie então usou as respostas das crianças para propor, pela primeira vez, cinco categorias sociais.

"Aceitas" e "rejeitadas" para aquelas que eram amplamente queridas ou rejeitadas, respectivamente.

"Controversas" para aquelas que recebiam um grande número tanto de "curtidas" quanto de "descurtidas".

"Negligenciadas" para aquelas que quase não eram mencionadas de nenhuma das duas formas.

E "medianas" para crianças que não se destacavam demais em nenhuma direção.

Muitos estudos confirmaram a utilidade desses rótulos. Em geral, eles mostram que cerca de 40% das crianças são "médias" e 60% se encaixam em uma das outras quatro categorias.

As crianças mais queridas tendem a ser vistas pelos colegas como gentis, incentivadoras e solidárias, enquanto as "negligenciadas" tendem a ser quietas e retraídas.

As crianças "rejeitadas" tendem a ser agressivas e praticam bullying contra os outros, ou são pouco assertivas, socialmente ansiosas e vítimas de bullying.

As "controversas", o grupo mais raro, dividem as opiniões, geralmente sendo vistas como os palhaços da turma ou os rebeldes.

Nos primeiros anos de escola , os valores das crianças costumam estar alinhados aos dos adultos que as supervisionam. No ensino médio, isso muda — Foto: Emmanuel Lafont/BBC

De maneira surpreendente, Coie descobriu que os rótulos atribuídos às crianças permaneciam, em grande parte, iguais mesmo quando elas eram apresentadas a novos grupos de colegas. E, embora a pesquisa inicial tenha sido feita com crianças do ensino fundamental, muitos estudos reproduziram os resultados com adolescentes. Um deles descobriu que cerca de metade das crianças mantém, cinco anos depois, no ensino médio, o mesmo rótulo que tinha no ensino fundamental.

"Eu tinha tido uma fase muito ruim no ensino fundamental, e sempre me lembro da minha mãe dizendo: 'Vai ser melhor quando você for para o ensino médio'", conta Connie*, outra amiga com quem conversei sobre experiência escolar. "Mas acho que, quando você sofre bullying, ou se tem alguma coisa que faz você parecer visivelmente diferente… É como se virasse um alvo fácil."

Depois de ser alvo de bullying nos primeiros meses do ensino médio, por motivos que incluíam não ser branca em uma instituição predominantemente branca, Connie mudou de escola. Na nova escola, porém, logo encontrou um padrão semelhante.

Embora os rótulos permaneçam os mesmos, a dinâmica social muda drasticamente entre o ensino fundamental e o ensino médio. No ensino fundamental, as crianças "populares" são simplesmente aquelas de quem os outros mais gostam, e muitas vezes as que se comportam bem e se destacam na escola, porque, nessa fase, os valores das crianças normalmente estão alinhados aos dos adultos que as supervisionam.

Os adultos e tudo o que eles representam se tornam profundamente indesejáveis. Um aluno consciente e extremamente dedicado pode acabar relegado à condição de "nerd", enquanto um aluno mais rebelde e divisivo pode, inesperadamente, ter uma ascensão social.

Conversando no telefone com o terror da minha escola, que agora é minha amiga próxima, Georgia, pergunto se ela se considerava popular no ensino médio. Ela diz que não pensava em si mesma dessa maneira.

"'Popular' dá a impressão de que as pessoas gostam de você, e não acho que necessariamente gostassem da gente", ela responde. "Talvez fosse mais uma coisa de ser… meio infame, sabe? Barulhenta e querendo chamar atenção."

Quando adolescente, Georgia encarnava o arquétipo da "controversa". Ela tinha comportamentos agressivos e perturbava as aulas. Para todos aqueles que a adoravam, provavelmente havia muitos que não gostavam dela. Digo a ela que as pessoas, inclusive eu, tinham bastante medo dela em determinado momento. Mas ela está errada ao achar que isso a desqualificava do rótulo de "popular".

Dadas as suas peculiaridades, é impressionante como usamos com tanta frequência o ensino médio como referência para as relações entre adultos — Foto: Emmanuel Lafont/BBC

"Nós começamos a prestar atenção em quem está recebendo mais atenção, quem pode ser mais dominante ou 'legal'", diz Prinstein. "Aqueles que começam a se tornar fisicamente mais atraentes, ou que se encaixam nas normas do grupo, [como] os que se vestem bem ou são bons nos esportes."

Adotar comportamentos "pseudomaduros", ações associadas a adolescentes mais velhos ou adultos, é outro caminho rápido para conquistar status. Adolescentes que bebem álcool, usam drogas e se envolvem precocemente em comportamentos românticos têm maior probabilidade de serem considerados populares — pelo menos por algum tempo.

Por volta dos 15 anos, esses comportamentos deixam de conferir status na mesma medida.

À medida que os adolescentes amadurecem, a busca explícita por status se torna menos vantajosa socialmente, e a "simpatia" começa a recuperar seu papel como importante determinante da posição social. Mas os efeitos dessas primeiras experiências de estratificação social extrema podem ser significativos.

"As experiências que temos quando somos crianças — se somos queridos, se somos populares ou temos alto status — parecem ter um efeito duradouro sobre nós mesmo 40 anos depois", diz Prinstein.

"Simpatia e status têm efeitos praticamente opostos. Ser querido é bom. Em geral, isso leva a todo tipo de resultado positivo na saúde, no trabalho, na vida acadêmica e na saúde psicológica.

"Mas ter alto status, na verdade, leva ao oposto."

Os pesquisadores costumavam pensar na cultura do ensino médio como uma versão imatura da sociedade adulta.

Mas, na década de 1960, começaram a entender que essa "cultura dos grupinhos" era algo muito mais estranho, um mundo paralelo movido por suas próprias fascinações excêntricas e conjuntos de códigos.

Em vez de uma simples hierarquia, o cenário social do ensino médio apresenta um sistema dinâmico de panelinhas. Os principais arquétipos se repetem na cultura popular, desde filmes como American Pie e Clube dos Cinco a seriados como Malhação: os populares, os desajustados, os rejeitados e os nerds.

Durante os primeiros anos do ensino médio, as fronteiras entre as panelinhas tendem a ser rígidas. "Os jovens podem se tornar extraordinariamente tribais, intolerantes e cruéis ao excluir aqueles que são 'diferentes'", escreveu o psicanalista germano-americano Erik Erikson em seu livro de 1959, Identity and the Life Cycle ("Identidade e o ciclo de vida", em tradução livre).

Essa intolerância, argumentava Erikson, talvez fosse "uma defesa necessária" contra a perda da identidade que se tinha quando criança, combinada a uma desconcertante onda de mudanças hormonais e à natureza avassaladora do futuro, com todas as suas possibilidades e escolhas.

Os adolescentes ajudam uns aos outros a atravessar esse desconforto "formando panelinhas e estereotipando a si mesmos", sugeriu ele. Essa classificação espontânea facilita a navegação dos adolescentes por seus mundos sociais, porque a "categoria" relativa de cada pessoa determina como ela deve ser tratada.

Uma coisa que é ignorada na cultura popular, porém, é a grande parcela de adolescentes que não aderem a nenhuma subcultura específica. Um estudo de 1985 descobriu que cerca de 45% dos alunos do ensino médio se definiam simplesmente como "normais". Enquanto os jovens populares diziam que sua vida girava em torno de estar bem-vestido e ir a festas, os "normais" que se autodefiniam assim diziam coisas como: "Sou apenas um adolescente comum".

Ser "anormal" e se destacar pelos motivos errados pode ser socialmente catastrófico. Connie se lembra de chegar à nova escola aos 13 anos e achar impossível conquistar um espaço naquela estrutura social escorregadia. Ela descreve suas tentativas de enfatizar diferentes aspectos de si mesma em busca da panelinha certa.

"Lembro de tentar fazer amizade com as meninas nerds. Lembro de tentar fazer amizade com as meninas legais", diz ela. "Eu pensava: 'Ah, sou muito estudiosa, faço toda a minha lição de casa'. E aí isso não funcionava, então era tipo: 'Ah, eu uso maquiagem, arrumo o cabelo', esse tipo de coisa. Tentei me encaixar com o pessoal da música. Comecei a tocar trompete."

Mas não adiantou. "Acho que eu sabia, no fundo, que simplesmente não estava funcionando", diz ela. "Não havia lugar para eu me encaixar. No fim, eu era completamente ignorada por todo mundo."

Perto do fim do ensino médio, a rígida hierarquia social começa a relaxar um pouco.

No início dos anos 1990, o pesquisador David Kinney realizou um estudo etnográfico no qual se inseriu em uma escola para observar de perto as mudanças nas fronteiras entre as panelinhas. Ele acompanhou antigos "nerds" que conseguiram fazer a transição para o grupo dos "normais".

A rigidez das panelinhas no início do ensino médio pode refletir as capacidades cognitivas limitadas dos adolescentes mais jovens, observou ele.

Embora os adolescentes mais novos estejam cada vez mais capazes de refletir sobre si mesmos, muitos não conseguem diferenciar entre a frequência com que pensam em si mesmos (muito) e a frequência com que os outros pensam neles.

Para muitos dos jovens "nerds" com quem Kinney conversou, isso resultava em uma atenção excessiva a si mesmos, debilitante, e em certa paralisia nas interações sociais.

Com o tempo, o desenvolvimento cognitivo permitiu que os antigos nerds se sentissem menos amedrontados e se cercassem de colegas que lhes ofereciam feedback positivo.

Se sentir "aceito", tanto no ensino médio como fora dele, é um dos mais fortes indicadores de resultados positivos na vida — Foto: Emmanuel Lafont/BBC

À medida que os adolescentes amadurecem, as barreiras que vêm da vontade de se encaixar começam a diminuir.

Os jovens populares podem até ser desafiados por colegas alternativos e rebeldes. O estudo de Kinney descobriu que, nos últimos anos da escola, os "moderninhos" eram desafiados por estudantes com "aparência extravagante e comportamento turbulento", que "competiam com eles pela popularidade em toda a escola".

Algumas dessas mudanças sutis já deviam estar acontecendo quando, aos 15 anos, Georgia me chamou pela primeira vez para sair com ela, mas ainda me lembro da confusão e da incredulidade que senti.

Naquela época, eu fazia parte de um grupo predominantemente masculino de maconheiros. Georgia estava tentando pregar algum tipo de peça em mim? Eu seria atraída para fora do meu grupo apenas para ser humilhada de alguma maneira?

Quase 20 anos depois, pergunto a Georgia por que ela queria ser minha amiga, algo que nunca havia perguntado antes. Fico pensando quais dos meus atributos extraordinários poderiam ter chamado sua atenção — minha inteligência, meu charme?

"Acho que havia uma estranheza que todos nós compartilhávamos", diz ela, hesitante. "Tipo, nenhum de nós era normal."

Dadas todas as suas peculiaridades, é impressionante como usamos com frequência o ensino médio como referência para nossas interações na vida adulta.

Quando Lucy Foulkes, psicóloga da Universidade de Oxford, no Reino Unido, e autora de Coming of Age: How Adolescence Shapes Us ('Chegando à idade adulta: como a adolescência nos molda', em tradução livre), publicou nas redes sociais um texto sobre o efeito das "garotas maldosas", recebeu uma enxurrada de pessoas dizendo que se identificavam.

"Muita gente dizia: não são apenas os adolescentes, eu vejo isso no ambiente de trabalho… Vejo isso entre as mães no portão da escola", diz Foulkes.

"É um fenômeno humano: algumas pessoas conquistam mais poder social e dominância sobre outras. Há algo particularmente intenso nisso durante a adolescência."

Foulkes observa que os adolescentes estão cercados pelas mesmas pessoas quase todos os dias durante anos, de uma maneira que "simplesmente não acontece na vida adulta, exceto no exército ou na prisão. Existe uma intensidade nesse ambiente que vai além do que está acontecendo dentro do cérebro deles".

É justamente essa intensidade que explica, em parte, por que essas experiências permanecem gravadas dentro de nós, diz Prinstein, moldando a maneira como interpretamos encontros sociais por muitos anos.

"Estamos recorrendo àquelas experiências de quando tínhamos 14 anos para usá-las como uma espécie de modelo através do qual enxergamos o mundo", diz Prinstein.

Ele aponta para estudos que sugerem que o modelo mental que usamos para processar nosso mundo social começa a se formar na infância e que as regiões do cérebro responsáveis pelo processamento da memória ficam ativas quando as pessoas pensam sobre comportamento social.

"Essas lembranças estão sendo trazidas de volta o tempo todo."

Muitos de nós provavelmente já nos perguntamos o que aconteceu com os "jovens legais" que conhecemos na adolescência.

Em um estudo de 2015, Joseph Allen, professor de psicologia da Universidade da Virgínia, nos Estados Unidos, tentou descobrir. Suas descobertas não foram muito promissoras para os jovens que um dia foram populares.

Acompanhando 184 adolescentes do sudeste dos Estados Unidos dos 13 aos 23 anos, Allen descobriu que jovens obcecados por status que adotavam comportamentos 'pseudomaduros' no início da adolescência apresentavam maior risco de enfrentar dificuldades de longo prazo em relacionamentos próximos, além de comportamentos criminosos.

A iniciação precoce ao álcool e às drogas estava associada a uma maior vulnerabilidade ao abuso de substâncias e a problemas de dependência mais tarde na vida.

E o foco no status desde cedo levava a vínculos mais superficiais e dificuldades para manter amizades e relacionamentos amorosos.

A experiência da rejeição também pode deixar cicatrizes. A pesquisa de Prinstein descobriu que alunos rejeitados no ensino médio tinham maior probabilidade de se tornarem mais deprimidos com o passar do tempo. Ele levantou a hipótese de que havia um ciclo de feedback negativo em ação, no qual a experiência de rejeição gera mais isolamento, que por sua vez intensifica os sentimentos de rejeição.

Em contraste, a "simpatia" — ser "aceito", tanto no ensino médio como fora dele — é um dos mais fortes indicadores de resultados positivos na vida, como uma carreira bem-sucedida, boa saúde e relacionamentos sólidos, até mesmo quando comparada a fatores como inteligência e origem socioeconômica.

Ainda assim, pessoas que vivenciam a rejeição também podem desenvolver qualidades importantes, como se tornar mais hábeis em identificar o que os outros estão sentindo ou mais conscientes de quando outras pessoas estão sendo maltratadas. Essa inteligência emocional já demonstrou ser útil para lidar com relacionamentos pessoais e com o mundo do trabalho.

E uma criança não precisa ser "aceita" para desfrutar de uma vida social satisfatória na idade adulta. Estudos descobriram que até mesmo ter um ou dois bons amigos na adolescência pode exercer um efeito protetor e fortalecer relacionamentos futuros.

O mais importante é que podemos manejar a maneira como nossas primeiras experiências nos afetam.

Segundo Prinstein, os roteiros sociais desenvolvidos no ensino médio que usamos para abordar as interações podem se tornar uma profecia autorrealizável.

"Quando entramos em um contexto social, podemos nos concentrar nas informações que confirmam nossas piores expectativas", diz ele. "Então, podemos nos comportar de maneiras que, na verdade, incentivem mais experiências negativas."

Ao escolher atualizar esses modelos (por exemplo: decidir que um comentário ambíguo de um colega provavelmente não tinha a intenção de nos chatear) podemos nos ajudar a ter experiências mais gratificantes, afirma ele.

Como uma adolescente que tinha alto status e que, desde cedo, adotava comportamentos arriscados e pseudomaduros, Georgia diz: "Sinto uma certa tristeza pela minha versão mais jovem, por nunca ter tido a oportunidade de simplesmente ser uma criança normal".

Ela conta que uma experiência precoce em que viu uma amiga ser espancada, combinada ao comportamento abusivo em casa, a convenceu a agir de forma agressiva para transmitir uma imagem de invulnerabilidade.

Ela lamenta não ter recebido mais apoio naquela idade e, em vez disso, ter sido rotulada pelos professores como uma "aluna problemática". "Isso moldou completamente minha trajetória profissional e minha defesa ferrenha das pessoas vulneráveis", diz ela.

Connie, por sua vez, diz que suas primeiras experiências de rejeição acabaram alimentando um padrão de autossabotagem.

"Acho que, de muitas maneiras, eu tinha desistido de mim mesma, e tinha tantos comportamentos autodestrutivos que acabou ficando difícil manter amizades", diz ela.

Isso culminou em um período de crise no fim da adolescência, do qual ela desde então tem trabalhado arduamente para se recuperar. Mais de uma década depois, ela descobriu o que ama, incluindo uma prática criativa e uma carreira gratificante, e diz que raramente pensa em seus dias de escola.

Tanto Connie quanto Georgia são uma prova de que os rótulos que carregávamos no ensino médio não precisam ser uma sentença para a vida toda.

"As pessoas podem absolutamente mudar o rumo das coisas", concorda Prinstein. "O problema é que não passamos muito tempo falando sobre isso... O que significa que temos maior probabilidade de repetir nossos padrões."

articles.title: RSPB marks 50 years at wildlife-rich Strumpshaw Fen
articles.summary: Reserve manager Helen Deavin says the site helps rare species not just survive, but thrive.
articles.body:
A nature reserve tucked away on the Broads and home to some of Norfolk's most threatened wildlife is celebrating 50 years.

Strumpshaw Fen covers 450 hectares (1,112 acres) of diverse wetland — the equivalent of 630 football pitches.

Reserves manager Helen Deavin said the site supported "rare and unusual species", including nesting bitterns, the swallowtail butterfly and a pair of cranes that successfully raised a chick this summer.

"One of the lovely things about Strumpshaw is that the wildlife is quite accessible," added Deavin, who called the reserve a "hidden gem".

Marsh harriers, bearded tits, flocks of waders and overwintering ducks and geese are a regular sight for visitors, along with otters, water voles, fen raft spiders, orchids and rare sharp-leaved pondweed.

"There's this incredible, really quite rare wildlife but actually it's really possible for people to see it, get some great views and really experience the magic of the Broads," added Deavin.

"By developing habitats where wildlife feels safe and can find the right food and places to shelter and raise a family, teams across the years have created a reserve that helps populations of rare species not only survive, but thrive."

She said the summer's heatwaves had been "tough", but they were hoping for a cooler, wetter autumn, with the reserve braced for flood events and "saline surges" with seasonal tides.

Strumpshaw is hosting various events to celebrate the milestone, including guided walks around the site on Sunday.

The reserve started off as unmanaged fenland and was taken over by the RSPB in the mid-1970s.

'It has become a place full of memories'

BBC Look East camera operator Shaun Whitmore has always loved Strumpshaw Fen and in his own words, he explains why.

Alongside that, Strumpshaw is somewhere I can take a step back to pause and think about my life.

In 2016, it was the place I went to, when everything in my life became too much for me. Nature provided me with a way out of the breakdown I was having at the time.

On my birthday, in December 2019, Strumpshaw Fen was the place I took my future wife to propose.

Maybe my timing was off, because we went into lockdown two days into the filming. I did make a film and it went out on Look East the following week, showing what we were all missing while we were having to stay indoors for a while.

I have beautiful memories of this stunning part of Norfolk, with its reed beds, grazing marshes, woodland area and river frontage, along with an abundance of birds and other wildlife.

It's a perfect place to relax and enjoy the fresh air and freedom that we all need in our busy lives.

articles.title: America’s biggest investor Michael Burry issues '$100 billion warning' on America's biggest defence tech company: Says will fall below ...
articles.summary: Tech News News: America’s biggest investor Michael Burry has renewed his criticism of Palantir Technologies, wanting that the valuation of the company could collapse .
articles.body: America’s biggest investor Michael Burry has renewed his criticism of Palantir Technologies, wanting that the valuation of the company could collapse below $100 billion. Despite Palantir’s AI-fueled rally that has lifted its market capitalisation to $407.2 billion, Burry argued the company resembles a consulting firm more than a true software business. “Palantir is back in the stratosphere. The facts have not changed,” he said in a post on X. Palantir shares slid 6% last week to close at $169.46, marking their worst session in over a week and tracking their weakest week in two months.Michael Burry feels that Palantir is riding a bubble of AI demand Burry described Palantir as “a consultant riding a bubble of AI FOMO demand.” He warned that even if the corporate scramble for AI lasts several more years, the eventual fall could be “epic, or more so.” His comments follow Palantir’s blockbuster Q2 results, which showed revenue surging 93% year-over-year to $1.94 billion and a raised 2026 outlook of $8.15 billion.Burry’s case centers on Palantir’s rising accounts receivable, which climbed to $1.49 billion as of June 30 from $1.04 billion at the end of 2025. He noted that one customer represented 27% of receivables despite no single client contributing more than 10% of revenue. He warned this concentration gives the customer significant leverage, raising risks of delayed payments or channel stuffing.Questioning the software labelBurry further argued that Palantir's deferred-revenue patterns look more like those of a consulting firm such as Accenture than a subscription software company like Salesforce or ServiceNow. He pointed to Palantir's deferred-revenue-to-revenue ratio of about 32% — close to Accenture's 31%, but far below the 80%-to-207% range he calculated for true SaaS peers — as evidence that the company isn't the software business its narrative suggests. He also cited an unverified private conversation among former Palantir employees describing the company's real "moat" as its willingness to staff clients with people working extremely long hours rather than software alone, with one participant reportedly dismissing its AIP branding as opportunistic.Stock compensation and tax benefitsBurry also took aim at Palantir's use of stock-based compensation and tax planning. The company reported about $1.6 billion in pretax GAAP income for 2025 but paid no federal cash taxes, thanks to net operating loss carryforwards that grew to $9 billion from $5.5 billion — an increase Burry attributed largely to deductions tied to stock compensation. He argued shareholders are effectively funding employee pay through dilution while the federal government subsidizes the company through substantial tax shields. He also flagged Palantir's decision to cancel a $1 billion buyback authorization after repurchasing only about $75 million worth of shares in 2025, alongside CEO Alex Karp's sale of roughly 492,000 shares worth $86 million last month.Alex Karp's private jet spendingBurry also criticized disclosures showing Palantir spent $17.2 million on expenses tied to CEO Alex Karp's personally owned aircraft in 2025, more than double the $7.7 million spent the year before. articles.title: 'Too hot for ice cream' - warmest summer's impact on trade
articles.summary: Figures from the UK and Channel Islands say the summer has been the hottest on record.
articles.body:
This summer's hot weather has led to mixed fortunes for businesses as they dealt with the positive and negative impacts of record-breaking conditions.

Some traders in south-west England and the Channel Islands said they benefitted from higher visitor numbers and increased demand for food and beverages, but others faced challenges as a result of prolonged dry conditions.

According to provisional data from the Met Office , the average mean temperature for June, July and August was 16.5C (61.7F), making it the warmest summer on record in the UK based on statistics stretching back to 1884.

Meteorologists in Jersey and Guernsey confirmed the islands had their warmest summers on record, with average temperatures for Jersey at 20.5C (68.9F) and 18.9C (66.2F) in Guernsey .

Ice cream seller Christian Hocking, from Hocking's in Appledore, Devon, said trade had been steady, but customers were choosing water over a sweet treat due to a lack of appetite in the heat.

He said: "When it gets too hot, it does actually gets too hot for ice cream."

Others who faced issues during the summer included Guernsey Dairy, with a spokesperson saying the dry spells and high temperatures affected milk volumes from local farms.

However, they added milk supplies remained sufficient to meet daily demand across the island.

Operations director Andrew Tabel said: "Our local dairy farmers and production teams have worked incredibly hard throughout this prolonged period of hot and dry weather."

In Devon, The Avon Inn in Avonwick reported a boost in trade, with manager Eda Iannone saying the pub had seen "a fantastic summer for footfall" after adding more outdoor seating.

She said: "We took a lot more bookings and we put a lot more outside events on with confidence, knowing that with the UK being weather dependent, they would go well."

Tina Bessell from Cornish Lavender, based between St Agnes and Perranporth, said the heat helped produce a "fantastic" oil yield, although visitor numbers to the site fell on the hottest days.

"The farm has loved the heat," Bessell said.

"I think I must be the only farmer in the South West that is happy with the heat."

But for cider producers Rocquette Cider in Guernsey, the hot weather is set to leave its apple harvest about 80% lower than normal, with manager James Miller describing it as "appalling".

Miller added: "The grass is very dry, we haven't had to mow the grass at all.

"The trees have been suffering, I think the only moisture they've been getting is from morning dew.

"Last year we had a good harvest, so we have a lot of cider stored which will carry us through, but two bad years would be devastating."

Jon Parks from the National Trust for Jersey said extreme weather was affecting St Ouen's Pond, with low water levels and algal growth threatening an important habitat for migrating birds.

"Normally at this time of year we'd have all sorts of visitors like green sandpipers, curlews and we've had spoonbills visit us at this time of year before," Parks said.

"They're all looking for that wetland habitat, a chance to feed and there's no water there, there isn't that opportunity unfortunately."

Parks said extreme summers were a "major contributing factor" to the problems, but he emphasised they were not the only cause.

articles.summary: Hayden Leigh, a forensic science graduate, is studying the hair of Boris the bear.
articles.body:
A student has been using hair from a 120-year-old museum exhibit to help find new ways of solving wildlife crime.

The taxidermy bear, known as Boris, is a popular feature at the Museum of Chelmsford and is regarded as its unofficial mascot.

Hayden Leigh, a forensic science graduate at the University of Staffordshire, is using samples taken from his hair to help protect modern-day brown bears from illegal poaching.

His PhD research involves analysing Boris's fur to compare how its characteristics could improve identification of animal hairs during investigations.

Boris arrived at the museum in 1932 amongst a large collection of taxidermy bequeathed by a local game hunter.

Leigh said in the wild the animals were mostly found in places like Romania and Bulgaria as well as Russia.

He said he had been using a microscope to analyse the cuticles, and different layers of the bear's fur as well as its DNA.

Leigh had previously approached about 30 zoos and museums for help with the project before the Museum of Chelmsford said they would lend a hand.

"There's been hundreds of studies done on dog hairs and cat hairs and general domestic animals, and I thought, well, let's make a wider impact than on the wider wildlife crime investigations," he said.

By developing more a cost-effective and reliable alternative to DNA analysis, the aim is to help tackle the illegal poaching and trafficking of wildlife.

"Taxidermy samples from museums can play a valuable role in the research of animal hair within a forensic context, Leigh added.

"They are often far more accessible than obtaining hair from live animals.

"In my project, I examined Boris's hair at a microscopic level, assessing the characteristics of the hairs and investigating whether there was any variation across different areas of the body."

Having access to a preserved specimen had also meant an opportunity to examine authentic animal hair in a controlled and ethical way, he said, without needing to disturb a live animal.

Councillor Jennie Lardge, cabinet member for culture and leisure at Chelmsford City Council, acknowledged that taxidermy was often considered a controversial part of museum collections, but said it was "wonderful" that Boris' legacy would be to help protect other animals from illegal hunting.

"It highlights the scientific value of historic taxidermy collections in museums in 2026, and we are delighted that the Museum of Chelmsford has been able to support this important project," she said.

articles.body: NEW DELHI: Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge on Sunday launched a sharp attack on Prime Minister Narendra Modi and accused him of turning his address at Delhi University's SRCC into "yet another political campaign" instead of facing questions from the youth.In a social media post on X, Kharge also attacked PM Modi for giving the opposition "a new adjective every" year, calling it his "modus operandi" to hide his own failures."Modi ji visited Delhi University's SRCC yesterday. articles.title: How social media is inspiring a new generation of bookworms
articles.summary: Whether it is viral novels or emerging subgenres, BookTok is influencing people's reading habits.
articles.body:
Social media is used by millions of people around the world to connect with friends, stay up to date with the latest pop culture news and for short-form entertainment, but one corner of the internet is encouraging a shift back to a non-digital pastime.

Discussing books and sharing reviews is by no means a new trend, but the social media movement of BookTok and Bookstagram which emerged in recent years has changed the way people showcase and share their reading habits.

The BookTok and Bookstagram communities on TikTok, Instagram and YouTube are made up of readers, authors and creators who share book-related content, including reviews, bookshelf tours and recommendations.

The phenomenon has led to viral titles, introduced some people to books and helped others to lower their screen time.

In pictures: River football and rescued cygnets

Driver in his 30s dies after car crashes into tree

'Miracle' crash survivor to scale Helvellyn peak

Among those is Mia, a 14-year-old keen reader from Bristol.

Although she watches book-related content on YouTube, she said her screen time was "definitely lower" nowadays due to the amount of time she spends reading.

Mia also credited her friends and their recommendations for influencing her to read more, including the romantasy series Powerless by Lauren Roberts which got her hooked on books.

"While reading it, I was on the edge of my seat wondering what was going to happen next.

"I've had such a cut from screen time like with Netflix and Disney+. I don't really go on those anymore because I think, well, what would I prefer to do? Watch a TV series or find out what happens next in my book?

"I think [reading] keeps my brain engaged. I find reading helps me do that because I'm in a different world.

"There's loads of different genres, so if you're not into one thing - like if you're not into mystery - don't give reading up because you might prefer romance or something."

Although it began online, the BookTok phenomenon can often be found in dedicated sections of many bookstores.

A BookTok chart was also launched earlier this year , which combined data from traditional charts like the Sunday Times bestseller list along with UK sales data and analysis of the #BookTok hashtag.

The inaugural chart was dominated by romance and romantasy books - the mixed genre of romance and fantasy that Holly Irwin dedicated her own bookshop to.

The 20-year-old, who relocated to the Cotswolds from Hamilton, New Zealand, earlier this year, began her Instagram account in 2021 to share reviews, find new books and connect with fellow romance fans.

Holly said she "never really got into reading" as a child and always thought books were not for her.

However, her interests changed during the Covid-19 pandemic when she read the Twilight saga.

"I loved the movies, so I started reading. I'd never really tried to read romance before that, so I thought books weren't for me.

"I read Twilight and I absolutely devoured those books and I haven't stopped since - it's been books, books, books," she said.

Holly's social media "took off" and exceeded 149,000 followers across Instagram and TikTok.

While on a trip to Oxford in 2024, Holly and her mum Maria discussed the idea of opening a bookshop specialising in romance novels.

"We got back home to New Zealand and just thought life's too short... you've got to follow your dreams and you've got to give it a go.

"We spent the last couple of years planning it all, figuring out how we wanted to do it and then we decided it was time.

"It was kind of all or nothing... it's been wild, but it's been so fulfilling and so worth it to see this dream of mine come true," Holly said.

According to the Publishers Association, the UK's publishing income hit a record high of £7.4bn in 2025.

The company said the nation's "increasing appetite" for fiction, children's books and audiobooks were among the factors behind the growth.

NielsenIQ BookData found that romance and saga book sales declined by 15% in 2025 with 10.1m units sold - a decline which comes after several years of exceptional growth.

However, the sales of the genre were still twice as high as they were in 2019.

Sci-fi and fantasy books - which encompass the romantasy subgenre - saw record sales last year, with a 42% increase year-on-year.

A total of 8.8m units were sold, which was a 183% increase on 2019, a spokesperson for the organisation said.

Since opening Hollyhocks in August, Holly said she had met local romance fans as well as many people who had made a journey to Cirencester to visit the specialist bookshop.

She also said she noticed specific titles and subgenres - like hockey romance and cowboy romance novels - selling out quicker than others.

"It's definitely because of BookTok… everyone has just been on such a cowboy romance kick.

"I think people like to escape to a whole different world, so that's definitely a contributing factor.

"It blows me away, the power of social media," she added.

articles.title: We feel abandoned by police in crimewave, say Kings Heath residents
articles.summary: A crimewave in part of Birmingham over several months leaves residents asking who is in control.
articles.body:
Working on a busy high street, staff at Subway in Kings Heath, Birmingham, are used to dealing with tricky customers.

Teenagers leaping over the counter to steal entire trays of crisps and cookies, however, is not something they were prepared for.

The fizzy drinks fridge has been ransacked numerous times over the summer, the front door and windows smashed. Customers who were unfortunate to witness the attacks have been verbally abused, with one also having his bike vandalised.

"We've had a number of staff leave recently," one worker says. "They should not have to come to work in fear."

Along the road at Greggs, the gang has rushed in to steal armfuls of food. On one occasion, a female worker who tried to lock the doors to stop them was assaulted by a teenage girl.

A convenience store has been targeted so often they have to keep the doors locked all evening, the manager says as he scrolls through CCTV images of thefts and vandalism.

At Coustis hair salon, where hairdressing siblings Tina Bartlam and Antonio Constantinou have been for 40 years, the windows are boarded up after being smashed.

Kings Heath is known for its good schools, independent shops, lively music and art scene and strong community spirit.

But in recent months, the actions of a few have caused many to feel unsafe and unsure of who is in control.

Community groups on Facebook are filled with eyewitness reports of crimes taking place almost daily, fuelling anger and questions about why no-one seems to be able to put to a stop to it.

Insp Hayley Thompson, who oversees policing in Kings Heath, said the force took anti-social behaviour "incredibly seriously" and they were working to make the area safer.

But Matt Powell from Enjoy Kings Heath, the area's Business Improvement District (BID), who has been taking calls from distressed shop owners for months, is sceptical.

"This community has been let down by the police," he says.

"People feel like they've been abandoned."

He has had a good relationship with officers over the years, but feels the lack of reassurance to the public about the recent crimewave has created a "vacuum" for people to consider vigilantism.

An even bigger problem, he says, is drug dealing taking place openly in the streets. Shoplifting is another major issue.

Powell says he understands the pressures of modern day policing and assumes something is happening behind the scenes they may not be privy to.

But "the lack of visible policing is surely making people feel like they can get away with it", he says.

In July, West Midlands Police and Crime Commissioner (PCC), Labour's Simon Foster, said £12.2m funding had paid for 150 new police officers in neighbourhood teams along with 20 police community support officers (PCSOs).

Another 139 officers are being redeployed into local teams to focus on a "prevention and problem solving approach".

Talking to people on the high street, they feel it was a mistake to shut Kings Heath police station. It closed for good in 2025, 10 years after its front desk stopped taking inquiries from the public.

Officers from the neighbourhood policing team are based just over a mile away at Moseley Police Station, but there are concerns Kings Heath falls down the list of priorities.

Others waiting to speak to police are the parents of four boys who were threatened with a knife at Kings Heath Park.

The boys, aged 11 to 14, had gone there in the early evening of 29 August while their parents were at a function in the Red Lion pub.

They were approached by three teenagers and a scuffle ensued. A youth brandished a knife and told one of the visiting boys to "get on your knees", which, terrified, he did.

"They managed to escape - my brother ran and knocked on the door of the nearest house but no-one was in so they ran back to the pub," the boy's older sister says.

Her 11-year-old son and his friend had run away in fear but found a couple walking their dog who returned them safely to their parents.

While they spoke with police on the night, the family says no searches or arrests were made in the area, and a week after the ordeal they have still not been contacted by officers.

The force told the BBC it was unable to comment on this case.

Recently installed Lime scooters and bikes near the new Kings Heath railway station have been spotted being used by children as young as 12, who are dangerously weaving in and out of traffic and kicking cars.

The bikes should only be ridden by over 18s and identification is required for anyone setting up an account.

Lime says it is working with police to help prevent underage riding and wants members of the public to report incidents to it.

It also urges adults not to unlock vehicles for children, adding it is a "shared responsibility".

The crimewave led Councillor Jordan Phillip to write a public letter to West Midlands Police asking for a meeting to discuss the force's plan of action.

"There is a growing perception among residents that the problem remains unaddressed and the situation is continuing unchecked," he wrote.

His Green Party colleague, Councillor Hamzah Sheikh, is the lead on anti-social behaviour for the ward and also sits on the West Midlands Police and Crime Panel.

"I've lived here for three years," he said. "It has changed to the point that people don't feel safe walking up the high street."

When asked if the area had been let down by police, he nodded.

"Neighbourhood policing is at breaking point," he says.

"They have a hard job and they don't have the resources to do what they've got to do."

A woman who was assaulted near the railway station says police have kept her informed during their investigation. Two shop owners say they have been visited by officers but agree much more needs to be done.

Sheikh says he has spoken to the parents of some of the youths accused of running riot.

One mother has received death threats, possibly triggered by anger on social media.

"The mother is distraught. She's doing everything she can," he says of the struggle to control her child's actions.

Many people are sympathetic and want to help. A number of residents say a multi-agency approach is needed - that it is not just about the police, but also education, structure and support from social services and the community.

Cleveland police chief proud of force but being 'let down' by funding

'I'd rather die than ring the police': Distrust and fear in Middlesbrough after A66 crash

Al Carns, the MP for Birmingham Selly Oak which includes part of Kings Heath, says he is well aware of problems, with more than 100 offences thought to have been committed by the same group.

"It started as petty anti-social behaviour pre-Christmas and has escalated to significant shoplifting and theft. We've got to put an end to it," he says.

He says neighbourhood officers have increased by 49% in a year, which is significant, and urges people to get in touch with him if they continue to have issues.

On Wednesday, two boys aged 13 and 14 were charged with theft of a motor vehicle as part of police's efforts to crack down on crime in the area.

The force said it could not respond to a number of questions from the BBC because of the live case.

"We want everyone to enjoy living or visiting Kings Heath and not be intimidated," Insp Thompson says.

"Making our communities safer is a priority for us and we'll continue to work with partners to achieve this."

The PCC says the "serious concerns raised have been immediately escalated to the Chief Superintendent of Birmingham Local Policing Area".

"I expect the local Neighbourhood Team to tackle the crime and anti-social behaviour as a matter of urgency," he added.

He said West Midlands Police had 500 fewer police officers and 500 fewer PCSOs than in 2010 but "the majority of other police force areas have more than they have ever had".

"I have been repeatedly calling on government to ensure our region receives its fair share of officers and funding for over five years, but unfortunately government will not listen and will not act," he said.

A Home Office spokeswoman says it is delivering "the biggest reforms to policing in over 200 years to allow forces to focus on protecting their community".

"Police force funding this year is at a historic high of £18.5bn, with West Midlands Police seeing a cash increase of 4.1%."

A wider review of the police funding formula will also take place to ensure it is "fair and responsive to local needs", a statement added.

The feeling of lawlessness has galvanised the community in many ways. A petition has been started urging authorities to work together to protect residents.

The councillors say they are committed to helping to turn things around.

"I'm fighting for this community. I want to be here for the rest of my life," Sheikh tells the BBC.

Coustis's Tina Bartlam says they have been feeling "abandoned and vulnerable" but that swift, hard work is needed to recover.

"This is redeemable, but it needs to be done quickly," she says.

articles.title: Durham litter pickers collect bags of rubbish from River Wear
articles.summary: A litter picking group gathers every month to remove rubbish from the River Wear in Durham.
articles.body:
A litter picking group which removes rubbish from a river collected more than 50 bags of rubbish at their latest gathering.

The Durham City Riverscape Community formed just before the coronavirus pandemic to carry out monthly litter picks along the River Wear.

The group estimated it had collected tonnes of waste from the water since the start, including a large fridge earlier this year.

Lead volunteer Graham Hollingwood said the group was approaching the 1,000 bag milestone which "just shows how much work goes into protecting our riverbanks" and the "phenomenal" efforts of volunteers.

He said pulling the full sized fridge freezer out of the river was their biggest challenge to date but the team proved equal to it.

"None of this incredible progress would be possible without the phenomenal, unwavering support of the City of Durham Parish Council," Hollingwood said.

"Their funding, practical backing, and ongoing encouragement give us the resources and confidence we need to keep getting out on the water, tackle massive fly-tipping hazards, and make a genuine, lasting impact on the local environment."

Clerk of the City of Durham Parish Council and co-founder of the litter picking group Adam Shanley said the scale of dedication from volunteers was "extraordinary".

"It is an absolute privilege for the council to support and stand alongside such a proactive, passionate team," he said.

"We will continue to back our volunteers every step of the way as they work tirelessly to safeguard the River Wear for generations to come."

articles.title: A 10-year-old started a wildlife project after finding a US park covered in trash; years later, he rescues turtles, pelicans and fish
articles.summary: US News: At just 10 years old, John Carl Tilghman encountered something during a family trip that changed the direction of his life, a US national park littere.
articles.body: At just 10 years old, John Carl Tilghman encountered something during a family trip that changed the direction of his life, a US national park littered with rubbish. Instead of simply walking past it, he and his brother began thinking about what they could do to protect the wildlife affected by human waste. That conversation eventually became Conservation Brothers, a hands-on conservation initiative focused on protecting natural resources and helping animals. Years later, Tilghman is still carrying that mission forward. Now a high school junior, he spends time rescuing fish, sea turtles and pelicans caught in discarded fishing line, installing monofilament collection bins and building nesting boxes for wood ducks.A family road trip sparked a conservation missionTilghman's journey began during a 2017 cross-country trip with his family, when he and his brother visited a national park and were shocked by the amount of rubbish scattered throughout the area. According to Points of Light, the experience stayed with the brothers after they returned home. They began discussing ways they could make a difference and eventually created Conservation Brothers, drawing on their family's previous experience with nonprofit work. What started as an idea between two children developed into a continuing programme of practical conservation activities. Rather than limiting their efforts to raising awareness, the brothers focused on projects they could physically carry out, including shoreline clean-ups, fishing clinics, wildlife protection and habitat improvement. For Tilghman, the early encounter with litter also became a lesson in how everyday human behaviour can have consequences far beyond what people see.Fishing line became an unexpected threat to Florida wildlifeAs Tilghman grew older, his conservation work became closely connected to his experience as a deckhand on a charter boat. Working offshore, he regularly encounters wildlife suffering from discarded fishing line. Fish can become tangled and need to be carefully freed before being returned to the water, while sea turtles and pelicans can become seriously entangled around docks and waterways. Tilghman told Points of Light that he has assisted with sea turtle rescues and encountered pelicans caught in fishing line almost daily at the dock. His response has gone beyond rescuing individual animals. Through Conservation Brothers, he builds monofilament fishing-line receptacles and helps install them at marinas and docks, giving anglers a safer place to dispose of unwanted line. The approach tackles the problem before it reaches wildlife, turning personal encounters with injured animals into a broader prevention effort.Wood duck boxes are helping rebuild lost nesting habitatOne of Tilghman's proudest conservation projects involves an animal that needs suitable nesting spaces to reproduce, the wood duck. After a Category 5 hurricane struck the area in 2018 and destroyed trees and nesting habitat, Tilghman and his family researched the species and began constructing wooden nesting boxes. Four were installed around their backyard, where they could watch the ducks return and raise their young each spring. Each nesting box can produce as many as two broods of 12 to 15 eggs during spring, meaning the project's four boxes can potentially contribute to hundreds of hatchlings. The Conservation Brothers later placed five additional boxes in a cypress swamp on their northern Florida property, where Tilghman says the local population grew dramatically. What began as habitat replacement after a hurricane has become an annual wildlife project that lets the family watch new generations emerge.A teenager's conservation work is becoming a lifelong missionTilghman's work now stretches well beyond the project that began when he was 10. Conservation Brothers continues to organise shoreline clean-ups, fishing clinics and habitat projects, while Tilghman remains directly involved in planning and carrying out its activities. His experiences have also shaped his ambitions for the future. Tilghman is considering careers in biology or environmental engineering, reflecting how closely conservation has become tied to his interests. He also hopes the organisation will continue after he leaves for college, with plans to eventually pass its responsibilities to two younger cousins who share his enthusiasm for the outdoors. His story is a reminder that environmental action does not always begin with a large organisation or an elaborate plan. articles.title: Egyptian TV presenter Sarah Khalifa sentenced to death in drugs case
articles.summary: Cairo court sentences TV host Sarah Khalifa and 11 others to death over drug trafficking ring.
articles.body:
A court in Egypt has sentenced television presenter Sarah Khalifa and 11 other people to death by hanging after convicting them of drug charges.

The Cairo criminal court issued the death sentences after the defendants were found guilty of forming an organised criminal gang specialising in procuring materials used in manufacturing narcotics, with the intent to traffic them, the state-linked Al-Ahram outlet reported on Saturday.

The court also sentenced nine co-defendants to life imprisonment and acquitted seven others in a case that involved 28 defendants and more than 750kg of narcotics.

Khalifa, 39, is best known for hosting the security and crime programme “Mission Impossible”, which aired on the private Al-Mehwar TV channel.

Khalifa was also a business owner, running a cosmetic surgery clinic and an event planning company, and maintained a significant social media presence with over two million Instagram followers.

Khalifa denied the charges and told investigators she had “never smoked a cigarette in my life” and declared her innocence.

Egyptian media reported that she was weeping and crying during the session, asking the court for mercy: “Please listen to me, sir. My parents raised me well; they are people who pray, and I don’t need drug money”

Prosecutors said the gang imported raw materials from abroad to manufacture synthetic drugs, storing them in residential properties. Members divided roles between procurement, manufacturing and distribution, authorities said. Investigators seized unlicensed firearms and ammunition alongside the narcotics.

The prosecution said the group used a residential property to store the materials and manufacture the drugs.

The verdict, issued after the court consulted Egypt’s grand mufti for his non-binding religious opinion as required by law in capital cases, can be appealed before the Court of Cassation. Under recent judicial reforms, defendants have two avenues of appeal, beginning with a request for retrial before an appeals court.

Khalifa was arrested in April 2025 as part of the investigation. In a separate case on Saturday, the same court sentenced her to three years in prison for assaulting and filming her driver.

Egypt imposes the death penalty for drug trafficking, terrorism and premeditated murder.

articles.title: In 2004, two Georgia Airmen sank Christmas trees to give Scout Lake’s fish protective cover; such habitat can concentrate fish near fishing piers
articles.summary: US News: In 2004, Airman First Class Gary Yates and volunteer Marilyn Rodgers transformed Scout Lake into a thriving fishing spot by sinking Christmas trees as fish habitats, boosting local angling opportunities.
articles.body: In the winter of 2004-2005, Airman First Class Gary Yates and a volunteer named Marilyn Rodgers lowered a used Christmas tree into Scout Lake on Robins Air Force Base in Warner Robins, Georgia, sinking it to create fish habitat, according to a Robins Air Force Base article on the program. Artificial ponds like Scout Lake lack the dead wood, logs, stumps and drift piles that naturally accumulate in natural ponds over decades. The absence of such structures leaves no room for small fish to hide from predators and for the entire aquatic chain to form and ensure a balanced game fishery. Placing Christmas trees in the water is an inexpensive way to address this issue: the dense web of needles and branches provides protection to the forage fish while attracting algae and aquatic insects on the outer branches where smaller fish can feed on them.Fisheries agencies responsible for managing such projects don't rely on attracting fish from long distances; instead, the goal is to concentrate nearby fish in a spot anglers can reach. As per the guidance provided by state agencies responsible for the conservation of wildlife resources, the attractors gather fish in a small area rather than drawing fish from a large distance and that is exactly the reason they are deployed close to the boat docks and fishing piers. That logic applies just as well to a small base lake as it does to a large reservoir: a tree sunk within casting distance of a pier turns a quiet stretch of shoreline into a spot anglers can actually reach and fish productively.A 1980 creel survey on Norris Reservoir measured the payoff for anglersIt is hard to give any proof about the efficiency of such structures for both anglers and fish, but the results of the creel survey conducted in the Norris Reservoir of Tennessee are an obvious exception. There, 1,435 fishing parties were interviewed over 7.5 months in 1980: 115 anglers who fished only attractor areas, 2,582 who fished only open water, and 358 who fished both types of areas. On average, there were 9.8 brush-pile attractors per each of 259 coves in the reservoir. Anglers who fished near the attractors caught more fish per hour and in total weight compared to anglers who fished open water and the biggest increase was noticed among anglers who fished crappie. The authors note that fishermen who used attractors fished more successfully, caught more fish per man-hour and kilograms per man-hour and crappie anglers fished best of all. This study, titled Effects of Fish Attractors on Sport Fishing Success on Norris Reservoir, Tennessee, was deposited in the University of Tennessee’s graduate research repository and remains one of the best pieces of evidence that concentrating fish at fixed points increases catching opportunities rather than merely relocating them.Sonar imagery later showed why material choice still mattersThe second, more recent study, carried out in two turbid Piedmont reservoirs in North Carolina (Lake Townsend and Lake Cammack) by biologists working for the North Carolina Wildlife Resources Commission, has employed dual-frequency identification sonar (DIDSON) to assess the longevity and efficiency of various fish habitat attractors. The habitat cubes created from PVC and corrugated plastic pipes were compared to the bundle of evergreen trees using the number of fish found near them. There were significantly more fish near each type of attractor than there were in the water without the attractor; however, according to the study's report, the evergreen tree bundles deteriorated much faster than the artificial attractors, losing substantial branch volume within the first year and showing major structural breakdown by the third year. The study was titled Evaluating the Effectiveness of Artificial Fish Habitat Designs in Turbid Reservoirs Using Sonar Imagery. More than 800 fish habitats have been placed in the state due to research similar to the aforementioned.The fish attractor map provided by the North Carolina Wildlife Resources Commission now shows more than 800 fish attractors in more than 60 bodies of water, some of which have attractor sites with markers while others don’t. The page containing the map offers buttons allowing users to download the visible attractor sites in GPX and CSV format. As the Norris Reservoir study suggests, an attractor’s value lies in keeping fish concentrated where anglers can reach them. The North Carolina sonar research adds a caveat: Christmas trees provide that effect quickly, but they need replacing every few years because they decay faster than synthetic structures.A small project with a familiar patternThere is little documentation that gives an exact account of how Yates and Rodgers picked their dropping site and how the base measured their success thereafter. However, the program is just one of those that follows the trend found in all kinds of bodies of water in the United States, from Tennessee Valley Authority lakes to municipal ponds, where free, biodegradable Christmas trees continue to offer fish protection, draw in predators and give fishermen a fighting chance at a Georgia base and beyond.Catch the latest World News and Live updates.
