articles.title: India's eye in the sky that never blinks: Inside GISAT-1A
articles.summary: News News: India achieved a significant space milestone after successfully launching GISAT-1A, also designated Earth Observation Satellite (EOS)-05, its advanced.
articles.body: India achieved a significant space milestone after successfully launching GISAT-1A, also designated Earth Observation Satellite (EOS)-05, its advanced Geo-Imaging Satellite, aboard a Geosynchronous Satellite Launch Vehicle (GSLV) Mk II rocket from the Satish Dhawan Space Centre in Sriharikota.The launch marks a redemption story of sorts for Isro. The original GISAT-1, launched as EOS-03 in August 2021, failed to reach its intended orbit after the launch vehicle's cryogenic upper stage did not ignite as planned. This time around, the mission has gone off without a hitch, giving India its first operational satellite in this specialised category.What makes GISAT genuinely different from most of India's other Earth observation satellites is where it sits in space. Unlike conventional remote-sensing satellites that orbit in Low Earth Orbit (LEO), circling the planet multiple times a day and capturing images only when passing over a particular location, GISAT-1A has been placed in a geosynchronous orbit roughly 36,000 kilometres above the Indian subcontinent.A geosynchronous satellite matches Earth's rotational period, meaning it appears to stay put over the same general region of the planet continuously. This is fundamentally different from Low Earth Orbit satellites, which move quickly relative to the ground and only get periodic glimpses of any given area, or Sun-synchronous satellites, which pass over the same spot at the same local time each day but still only for a brief period.GISAT's persistent positioning allows it to keep a near-constant eye over the subcontinent, trading off some spatial resolution for continuous, real-time coverage. It represents a genuinely different design philosophy from Isro's typical Earth-imaging fleet.This persistent vantage point is what makes the satellite so useful for what is called remote sensing — the science of gathering information about the Earth's surface, atmosphere or oceans without any physical contact, typically using sensors that detect reflected or emitted electromagnetic radiation.Remote-sensing satellites act as very sophisticated cameras in the sky, capturing data across different wavelengths of light, including those invisible to the human eye, to reveal information that a regular photograph never could: soil moisture, vegetation health, water bodies, mineral deposits or the thermal signature of a wildfire.GISAT itself operates using multi-spectral and hyperspectral imaging, capturing data across a wide range of wavelength bands rather than just the visible spectrum. This allows scientists to distinguish between different types of land cover, crops, water quality or atmospheric conditions with far greater precision than a standard optical image would allow.The satellite is designed to deliver a sector-specific image of a selected area roughly every five minutes, and a complete image of the entire Indian landmass approximately every 30 minutes, at a spatial resolution in the tens of metres, while military satellites usually have a resolution of less than a metre.In practical terms, this gives Indian agencies something they have never really had before: an almost real-time, continuously updating picture of the country from space.EOS-05 plugs a long-standing gap in India's space-based Intelligence Surveillance and Reconnaissance grid, persistent surveillance. Most of our satellites sit in low earth orbit, which means excellent resolution but only fleeting passes over any given target. A geosynchronous platform like this flips that trade-off, you sacrifice some resolution, but you gain the ability to watch the same stretch of territory continuously, without interruption. On its own, that resolution limits its use for precision military tasking. But used alongside the LEO constellation, EOS-05 essentially becomes the overwatch layer, it flags where to look, and the higher-resolution LEO assets come in to confirm and detail. That combination, persistent wide-area watch plus high-resolution tasking, is really what a mature space-based surveillance architecture looks like.The applications this space-based asset unlocks are considerable. In disaster management, satellites like GISAT can track the formation and movement of cyclones, monitor flood extents as they develop, spot cloudbursts forming over vulnerable Himalayan regions and detect forest fires in their early stages — all crucial for issuing timely warnings and directing relief efforts more effectively.In agriculture, frequent imaging allows for crop health monitoring, yield estimation and drought assessment across growing seasons. The same data feeds into oceanography, glacier and snow-cover monitoring, mineral exploration, urban planning and, notably, security surveillance along India's borders and coastline — an application New Delhi has increasingly prioritised given the country's evolving security environment.India's journey into remote sensing did not begin with GISAT, of course. It stretches back to March 1988, when Isro launched IRS-1A, the country's first indigenous remote-sensing satellite, from the Soviet Baikonur Cosmodrome.That satellite, carrying relatively basic imaging sensors by today's standards, was designed to build India's foundational expertise in satellite imagery. It worked considerably better than expected, operating for four years against a planned mission life of three.It was followed over the subsequent decades by an expanding family of Indian Remote Sensing satellites, IRS-1B, IRS-1C and beyond, along with the RISAT series, which introduced radar imaging capable of seeing through cloud cover and darkness — something optical satellites simply cannot do.Altogether, India has launched around 40 dedicated remote-sensing and Earth observation satellites over the decades, though a significant number of the earlier ones have since completed their operational lives and been retired or deactivated.This steady accumulation of satellites and expertise matters a great deal for India's broader standing as a space power. Each new generation of Earth observation satellite, from the earliest IRS missions to today's GISAT, has progressively expanded what India can see, how quickly it can see it and how precisely it can interpret what it sees.This translates directly into greater self-reliance in critical areas like disaster response, food security planning, environmental monitoring and national security, reducing dependence on foreign satellite data for functions that are often too sensitive or too time-critical to outsource.GISAT-1A, sitting in its geostationary perch and watching over the subcontinent around the clock, effectively adds a persistent, always-on layer to this capability that India previously did not possess, complementing the periodic snapshots that its Low Earth Orbit satellites have long provided.With GISAT-1A now operational, India's space-based observation capability takes a genuine step forward — one that could prove its worth the very next time a cyclone forms in the Bay of Bengal, a forest catches fire in the Himalayan foothills or floodwaters begin rising somewhere across the country's vast and varied landscape.At the same time, India is building a robust military space architecture, expanding the largely civilian space programme with a sanctioned 52-satellite constellation under Space Based Surveillance Phase III, to be rolled out between 2025 and 2029.Notably, 31 of these satellites will be built by private industry, reflecting the growing role commercial players are being given in national security space programmes under the revised Space Policy 2026.The constellation aims to deliver persistent surveillance, secure communications and space situational awareness to monitor India's borders and maritime approaches. It is anchored in the Joint Military Space Doctrine announced at the 2025 Combined Commanders' Conference in Kolkata, which formally recognised space as a contested warfighting domain.Instead of relying on a handful of large satellites, India's upcoming space architecture uses a proliferated Low Earth Orbit design. The country will deploy dozens of smaller, agile satellites to reduce vulnerability to anti-satellite weapons and ensure redundancy.These satellites will carry hybrid payloads combining synthetic aperture radar and high-resolution optical sensors for round-the-clock, all-weather monitoring. Besides these, the satellites will also provide secure communication links.India is simultaneously developing counter-space capabilities, including electronic warfare and kinetic options. This includes the anti-satellite weapon system demonstrated by the country.

articles.title: Bodies of missing French fishermen recovered from Channel
articles.summary: Their boat sank off the coast of Plymouth after reporting problems with its fishing gear.
articles.body:
The bodies of two French fishermen who had been missing since their trawler sank in the English Channel have been found, French prosecutors have said.

The Maranello trawler sank off the coast of Plymouth on 29 August after reporting problems with its fishing gear, with three of the five crew members rescued by a nearby vessel.

Alex Dehays, deputy prosecutor in Saint-Brieuc, said divers found and recovered the bodies on Saturday after weather conditions allowed searches to resume.

The five-man crew raised a distress call at about 18:00 BST on 29 August.

A nearby fishing vessel, the Stradale, rescued three crew members before the Maranello sank.

The search for the missing fishermen involved UK and French rescue teams in waters south-west of the Eddystone Lighthouse, off Plymouth.

Poor weather delayed dives to the vessel after it was found.

articles.title: In 2009, an Arkansas tree seller supplied 500 Christmas trees for fish habitat in Greers Ferry Lake; volunteers turned them into 25 brush piles across three underwater areas
articles.summary: US News: In a creative environmental initiative, 500 discarded Christmas trees from Arkansas were repurposed as fish habitats in Greers Ferry Lake, creating new underwater shelters for fish and enhancing fishing opportunities.
articles.body: In early 2009, around 500 unsold and discarded Christmas trees in Arkansas were on their way to an unusual destination. The trees were headed for the bottom of Greers Ferry Lake. A Christmas-tree seller from Heber Springs named Harold McFarlin donated the trees for a fish-habitat project, where officials and volunteers of this project bundled them together and sank them at selected locations in the reservoir. The objective of this project was to create an underwater cover for young fish and baitfish while giving anglers new structures around which sportfish could be gathered.The Arkansas Game and Fish Commission (AGFC), the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, and members of the Greers Ferry Bassmasters came into a joint partnership for this project. Instead of treating the trees as post-holiday waste, the organisations decided to use them as a readily available source of woody cover.How 500 Christmas trees turned into underwater coverInstead of being sunk individually, the donated trees were bundled together. Workers loaded those bundles onto a front-loading dump barge donated by Bass Pro, which could be used to transport the materials out onto the lake before the trees were dropped to their designated locations.Reports suggest that the structures were intended to provide cover for newly born fish, minnows and shad. Those smaller fish populations were considered an important prey for larger sportfish, including bass, crappie and walleye. So, adding shelter for those smaller fish could make the structures useful parts of the lake’s fishing habitat.Later guidelines from the AGFC reflect why trees are bundled together. They explained that although Christmas trees can provide fish cover, their small branches and needles would generally deteriorate within about a year or two; thus, they recommended sinking them in groups because larger woody portions can continue to provide structure after the final material has decomposed.The placement also had to consider the lake’s recreational use, so brush piles were positioned deep enough to avoid interfering with boat traffic, even when water levels were low. This allowed the organisations to add the structures without turning them into navigation hazards.Three major areas were mapped for anglersFisheries Biologists identified that Sandy Beach, Devil’s Fork and Frontier Canyon needed additional underwater habitat. The 2009 operation created 25 brush piles across the three areas: 8 at Sandy Beach, 10 at Devil’s Fork, and 7 at Frontier Canyon. The crew also recorded the new structures with Global Positioning System equipment. The locations were intended to be made available to the public through the Corps of Engineers, giving the anglers a way to locate the newly established habitat rather than having to discover the brush piles themselves.This strategy of installing structures underneath continued beyond the 2009 Christmas tree project. For instance, in 2015, the Corps and local volunteers placed additional structures in Higden Bay using PVC pipes and cedar trees. Authorities explained that such structures could attract algae, small insects and baitfish. This, in turn, could attract larger fish and anglers.Post-holiday waste turned into a fisheries resourceThe Christmas-tree efforts were considered a part of a wider practice in Arkansas. The Corps had reportedly encouraged the community around Greers Ferry Lake to donate live, undecorated Christmas trees after the holiday season. In its 2013 programme announcement, the organisation shared that trees would be bundled into fish shelters and placed in the lake, with drop-off locations including Sandy Beach, Devils Fork and Choctaw Park.Thus, the operation that began with 500 discarded Christmas trees became 25 mapped underwater brush piles spread across three parts of Greers Ferry Lake, and prompted the officials to continue the same strategy as part of the lake’s broader fish-habitat programme for years to come.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: In 1984, Lou Dobbs acquired a New Jersey farm and expanded it over four decades; now the 283-acre estate with an 11-acre pond and development potential is listed for $6 million
articles.summary: US News: A large 283-acre farm built up over four decades by the late television anchor and radio host Lou Dobbs has been put on the market for $6 million. Kno.
articles.body: A large 283-acre farm built up over four decades by the late television anchor and radio host Lou Dobbs has been put on the market for $6 million. Known as Hickory Hollow Farm, the estate is located at 112 Quarry Road in Sussex County’s Wantage Township, near the New Jersey border with New York. The property includes an 11-acre spring-fed pond, extensive horse facilities, several guest homes and land with possible residential development potential, according to the New York Post and WRNJ Radio. Dobbs, a founding figure at CNN who later hosted Lou Dobbs Tonight on Fox Business, died in July 2024 at the age of 78. He first bought part of the property in 1984. Over the next 40 years, he continued buying nearby parcels, turning the land into one of the largest connected private farms in northwestern New Jersey. The property is currently listed by real estate agent Jaime Luongo of Weichert Realtors, according to listing documents cited by local media.Main residence and estate amenitiesAt the centre of the estate is a 5,419-square-foot colonial-style main house built in 1977. The home has five bedrooms and four bathrooms, along with a large kitchen, private office, sunroom and family room with a double-sided fireplace. Large windows across the main living areas provide views of the central 11-acre pond and the surrounding rolling pastures. Two bedrooms are located on the ground floor, while the second floor has the main bedroom suite, two more bedrooms and additional flexible living space. The main house is surrounded by several leisure facilities, including a four-car garage, a heated in-ground Gunite swimming pool, a full tennis court and a half-court basketball area. The property also has separate accommodation, including a two-bedroom, two-bathroom guest house and a two-bedroom, one-bathroom caretaker’s cottage.Professional equestrian infrastructure and working groundsHickory Hollow Farm was designed to operate as a large horse breeding and training facility. The main horse barn has 11 large stalls, a wash area, feed room, hay room and storage loft. The main barn connects directly to a sand riding ring. A second barn has three oversized stalls. Across the property are 17 grass paddocks with turnout sheds, a 150-by-200-foot fenced riding arena and an equipment garage for farm machinery. Beyond the managed pastures, the 282.72-acre property includes wooded areas, natural mountain views and a freshwater stream. The estate uses a private well, septic system and propane gas for its utilities. Public tax records included in the listing show that annual property taxes for the farm are about $37,000.Four-decade assembly and land potentialDobbs bought his first piece of land in Wantage Township in the mid-1980s while building his career as a founding anchor and managing editor of CNN’s financial reporting division. Over the years, the farm became both a working horse property and a private retreat where Dobbs hosted major seasonal gatherings, including annual Fourth of July events. The estate’s zoning and layout give potential buyers several options. The land could continue to be used for horse-related and agricultural activities, become a private family compound or potentially be divided for residential development, subject to approval from local authorities. The $6 million asking price works out to about $1,107 per square foot for the main living structures, while also reflecting the value of the entire 283-acre property. The listing comes after the earlier sale of Dobbs’ second home in West Palm Beach, Florida. That property was listed for $2.9 million shortly before his death in 2024.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: German minister outlines plans to improve drone and cyber security
articles.summary: German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt outlined plans to increase the country's defences against hybrid Russian attacks following a recent failed drone...
articles.body:
German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt outlines plans to increase defenses against hybrid Russian attacks following a failed drone attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport.

Dobrindt warns that Russia's hybrid attacks, including drones, cyberattacks, and sabotage, are a daily reality, but believes Germany can defend itself.

Specific plans to improve protection against drones and hacker attacks include deploying new units to protect critical transport hubs and establishing a national "Cyberdome" to detect and intercept hacker attacks.

German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt outlined plans to increase the country's defences against hybrid Russian attacks following a recent failed drone attack at a major airport in remarks to the Sunday edition of the mass-circulation Bild tabloid.

"Russia's hybrid attacks involving explosive-laden drones targeting airports, agents operating in our cities, cyberattacks on our networks, and sabotage of our infrastructure are a daily reality," Dobrindt said.

He predicted that the attacks would increase but said Germany could defend itself.

The newspaper reported on specific plans to improve protection against drones and hacker attacks, citing information from the Interior Ministry.

The airspace over critical transport hubs, airports, railway stations, and Berlin's government district was reported to be fully protected against drones by means of "new, rapidly deployable units," it said.

Companies operating critical infrastructure, such as water utilities, electricity providers, and defence contractors, are also to be given legal authority to actively defend themselves against drones.

A national protective shield known as a "Cyberdome" is to be established, comprising a dense network of digital sensors designed to detect and intercept attempted hacker attacks.

A drone laden with explosives was intercepted at Leipzig/Halle Airport near Ukrainian transport aircraft in August.

articles.title: Israeli flags become the latest weapon of settlers in West Bank domination
articles.summary: Israel’s visual colonisation aims to make Palestinians feel like guests in their own homeland.
articles.body:
A profound sense of anguish accompanies 25-year-old Taghreed Yahya during her daily commute from her town of Kafr Ra’i to the city centre of Jenin in the north of the occupied West Bank.

Along the main road connecting Jenin and Nablus, she is routinely confronted by hundreds of Israeli flags, a jarring visual imposition of Israeli domination and occupation on a route heavily used by local Palestinians.

Yahya said it started with a flag here, an outpost there, a new road cutting through the landscape.

“[It] makes the scene that was familiar for years change; all of this naturally leaves sadness, anger and fear, in addition to a feeling of helplessness,” she told Al Jazeera. “But at the same time, it strengthens the clinging to the land, memory and identity.”

This aggressive visual display of Israeli occupation represents an escalating phase of colonisation, extending beyond the physical outposts and attacks to a forced disfigurement of the geographical identity of the Palestinian territory.

When dozens of olive trees owned by the Palestinian residents of Arrabeh were uprooted, groups of Israeli settlers simultaneously decked a bypass road in northeastern areas of Jenin with Israeli flags to assert their dominance.

These flag-hanging campaigns, often facilitated by Israeli military incursions to secure the area, aim to artificially alter the Palestinian landscape. This is done in conjunction with the rapid deployment of mobile homes to establish dozens of settler outposts in new areas of the occupied West Bank.

For Palestinians who commute through this territory to work or home, the erasure of familiar landscapes is disorienting.

Faten Abdel Hadi, a photographer who regularly travels between Qalqilya, Nablus, Tulkarem and Salfit, noted that drastic changes materialised between June and August.

“I was hit by a lack of understanding of the geography I know, if I may say so. The major change that befell the most prominent landmarks in the streets seemed as if it went through a long time period, but it actually needed less than two months,” Faten told Al Jazeera.

“This scene is very painful: the scenes of the settlers’ mobile homes and flags, and their gatherings on the sides of the main streets, return us to the truth that these people stole our right and our belonging.”

This phenomenon escalated after October 7, 2023, when illegal settlement expansion and Israeli military raids in the occupied West Bank escalated. Israeli forces and settlers have killed more than 1,100 Palestinians since then, while a 66th Palestinian village was ethnically cleansed, according to B’Tselem.

Israel’s tender for buildings in the E1 settlement near Jerusalem also threatens to split the occupied West Bank in two, and analysts say it will end any hope of the establishment of a Palestinian state.

The process of Israeli expansionism often begins with the hardline group Hilltop Youth erecting a single tent or grazing sheep on a Palestinian hill, before larger illegal Israeli settlements are established in the area with government backing.

The Colonization and Wall Resistance Commission (CRRC) reported that Israeli authorities reviewed 113 structural plans to expand or establish new illegal settlements during the first half of 2026. This appears to mark a strategic shift by the Israeli government to produce new settlements on a mass scale to enforce Israeli sovereignty and annex Palestinian land.

Khaldoun al-Barghouthi, head of Israeli affairs and researcher at the Palestinian Research Center (PRC), said the deployment of Israeli flags to these areas is a tactic to enforce Israel’s physical and psychological presence in Palestinian areas.

The message to Palestinians is that Israeli settlers are a permanent fixture on the land, while their presence is temporary.

This localised intimidation is echoed by the highest echelons of Israeli leadership, including Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who recently boasted about building 104 illegal settlements and 160 settlement farms. His far-right ministers – Bezalel Smotrich and Itamar Ben-Gvir – have also used their powers to bolster the settlers’ expansionist aims.

“The control they are working on is not limited to fieldwork, meaning building settlements, confiscating lands and reducing the area of land owned by Palestinians, but also aims to sear the Palestinian consciousness regarding their existence on their land,” al-Barghouthi explained to Al Jazeera.

Ultimately, this psychological warfare serves a demographic objective. The overarching plan of the Hilltop Youth and the architects of the recent settler pogroms against West Bank villages is to force Palestinians to migrate from their rural communities. The result would be Palestinians confined to isolated urban areas, while the physical and visual landscape of the West Bank is entirely consumed by Israeli settlers and the military.

articles.title: Seattle opened light rail across the I-90 floating bridge in March; five months later about 2,000 fish have died near electrical equipment hanging into Lake Washington
articles.summary: US News: When Sound Transit launched light rail service across the I-90 floating bridge in March 2026, it was celebrated as a major milestone for Seattle’s tra.
articles.body: When Sound Transit launched light rail service across the I-90 floating bridge in March 2026, it was celebrated as a major milestone for Seattle’s transit network. For the first time, trains connected downtown Seattle to the Eastside over Lake Washington, promising faster commutes and reduced traffic. Five months later, that success story has been complicated by an unexpected environmental problem. Around 2,000 fish have been found dead near electrical cables and equipment that hang beneath the bridge into the lake. As reported by Axios Seattle, the deaths have raised concerns among biologists, regulators and local residents about how transit infrastructure interacts with one of the region’s most important bodies of water.A new rail line over a sensitive lakeThe I-90 floating bridge is an engineering marvel, a series of concrete pontoons tethered across Lake Washington that carry one of the busiest highways in the Pacific Northwest. When Sound Transit added a light rail line to the bridge, it required new electrical systems to power the trains. Some of that equipment, including cables and related hardware, extends below the bridge deck into the lake.Lake Washington is home to a variety of fish species, including kokanee salmon, cutthroat trout and other native and stocked fish. The lake is also heavily used for recreation, with boats, swimmers and anglers sharing the water year-round. Any large-scale fish die-off in such a visible, heavily used lake quickly draws public attention.What workers and boaters began to noticeIn the weeks after light rail service began, maintenance crews and boaters started reporting clusters of dead fish near the bridge. The fish were often found floating or washed up close to the areas where electrical cables and other transit equipment hang into the water. By late summer, the number of reported deaths had reached about 2,000, according to Sound Transit and state wildlife officials.The timing and location of the deaths suggested a link to the new rail infrastructure. While fish kills can happen for many reasons, including natural causes, disease or low oxygen levels, the concentration of deaths near the electrical equipment pointed to a more specific cause.The suspected role of electrical equipmentInvestigators from Sound Transit, the Washington Department of Fish and Wildlife and other agencies began examining the bridge’s electrical systems. Early findings suggest that some fish may be coming into contact with energised components or experiencing stress from electrical fields generated by the equipment. In some cases, cables or connectors that were intended to be insulated or shielded may be exposing fish to currents that can injure or kill them.The exact mechanism is still under study. It could involve direct electrocution when fish touch live parts, or more subtle effects such as disorientation, muscle spasms or physiological stress caused by electromagnetic fields. Whatever the precise cause, the outcome is the same: large numbers of fish dying in a small area near the bridge.Why this matters for Lake WashingtonLake Washington is not just a scenic backdrop for Seattle. It is a working ecosystem that supports fisheries, wildlife and recreational activities. A die-off of this size, concentrated in one area, can have ripple effects. Predatory fish and birds that rely on smaller fish for food may lose an important source of nutrition. Anglers who fish near the bridge may see reduced catches. And the sight of dead fish floating near a major piece of public infrastructure undermines confidence in how well the project was planned and monitored.There is also a symbolic dimension. The light rail expansion was promoted not only as a transportation improvement but as a step toward a more sustainable region. If that same infrastructure is harming the lake’s fish, it creates a tension between transit goals and environmental stewardship that officials will need to address.The response from Sound Transit and regulatorsSound Transit has acknowledged the fish deaths and says it is working with state and federal agencies to investigate and mitigate the problem. Initial steps have included:Inspecting the electrical equipment beneath the bridge for faults, exposed wiring or inadequate shielding.Monitoring fish mortality on an ongoing basis to track whether the problem is continuing or worsening.Coordinating with fish and wildlife biologists to study the health of the affected fish and test for electrical injury, disease or other causes.Regulators have made clear that they expect Sound Transit to take swift action. If the equipment is found to be noncompliant with environmental permits or wildlife protection laws, the agency could face orders to modify or shut down certain components until the issue is resolved.Possible solutions and their difficultiesTo fix this you need to balance intelligent engineering with what actually works day-to-day. Teams are exploring several potential fixes:Improved insulation: Heavy-duty shielding for submarine cables and hanging connectors.Rerouting hardware: Moving electrical components so that fewer of the parts are directly in the water.Fish deterrents: Installing physical barriers to keep marine life away from high-risk zones.Operational changes: Lowering power levels where feasible without impacting train safety.None of these solutions are simple, and each brings its own set of trade-offs. Adding extra shielding or redesigning equipment gets expensive fast and almost certainly means temporary train delays. Barriers might block natural water flow or look unsightly. And all changes need to be thoroughly tested before being deployed. The last thing anyone wants is a fix that causes more headaches for local wildlife, boaters or train operators.Bigger lesson for infrastructure projectsThe I-90 fish kills are a reminder that even infrastructure projects built with sustainability in mind can have unintended environmental consequences. Models and studies carried out in the planning phase may not accurately predict wildlife responses to new structures in real-world conditions. Fish behaviour, water currents and long term wear on equipment can all create surprises once a project is operating.For future transit and bridge projects in sensitive waters, the Seattle case is likely to be cited as a reason to build in more monitoring, more conservative design margins and clearer plans for rapid response if problems emerge. It also highlights the value of independent oversight and the need for agencies to be willing to pause or adjust operations when environmental harm becomes apparent.What happens nextIn the short term, the focus is on stopping the ongoing fish deaths. Sound Transit and its partners will continue inspections, testing and monitoring through the fall. If a specific fault or design flaw is identified, repairs or retrofits could begin as soon as parts and crews are available.The incident could lead to changes in how Sound Transit designs and maintains electrical systems on floating bridges and other lake crossings in the longer term. It could also affect the permitting for future projects with tighter rules on underwater electrical equipment and more rigorous monitoring after construction.For Seattle, a test of valuesFor many Seattle residents, the fish deaths near the I-90 bridge are more than a technical problem. They are a test of how the region balances progress and protection. Light rail is a point of pride, a symbol of a city investing in alternatives to cars and congestion. Lake Washington is also a point of pride, a place where people swim, boat, fish and find respite from urban life.The challenge now is to show that both can coexist. Fixing the electrical issues, being transparent about what went wrong and taking responsibility for the environmental impact will be essential if the public is to trust that the region’s push for more transit does not come at the expense of the waters that define it.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: 11 killed, seven injured as fuel tanker crashes, explodes in western Iran
articles.summary: Middle East News: A fuel tanker exploded in western Iran, killing 11 people and injuring seven others on Saturday, state media reported.According to IRNA, the tanker hi.
articles.body: A fuel tanker exploded in western Iran, killing 11 people and injuring seven others on Saturday, state media reported.According to IRNA, the tanker hit several other vehicles before bursting into flames near a traffic police station close to the Kurdish city of Sanandaj, around 400 km (248 miles) west of Tehran.The report attributed the accident to a faulty brake system. The injured were taken to nearby hospitals for treatment, AP cites.The tanker was traveling from Hamadan toward Marivan when a technical failure in its braking system caused the accident, according to the governor and cited by Iran International in its report.Similar accident killed 15 in 2018The latest incident comes after a similar road accident near Sanandaj in 2018, when a fuel tanker collided with an intercity passenger bus, killing 15 people and injuring four others.Road and traffic accidents kill more than 17,000 people in Iran every year. Experts have attributed the country's high road fatality rate to unsafe vehicles, violations of traffic rules and inadequate emergency services.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: ‘Adjacent building also caved in’: Eyewitnesses recall Delhi collapse horror in Satya Niketan
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: A building collapse in Delhi’s Satya Niketan area on Sunday left several people feared trapped under the rubble, with an eyewitness describ.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: A building collapse in Delhi’s Satya Niketan area on Sunday left several people feared trapped under the rubble, with an eyewitness describing a horrific scene in which an adjacent building also collapsed.The eyewitness said the collapsed structure, known as ‘Hostel Daze’, was a five-storey building being used as a boys’ paying guest accommodation. The person said another building next to it also collapsed, leaving students trapped beneath the debris.“The building that collapsed is called 'Hostel Daze'. Right next to it is another building that collapsed. 'Hostel Daze' is a dedicated boys' PG; it was a five-story building. The adjacent building also collapsed,” the eyewitness told news agency ANI.“All the students who were inside their rooms got trapped under the rubble,” the eyewitness added, saying the exact number of people trapped would only be known after checking the hostel’s registration records.Rescue teams were rushed to the site soon after the collapse, with the Delhi Fire Service deploying eight fire tenders along with multiple rescue teams from different departments.“The fire brigade and rescue teams have been at work for about 15-20 minutes—ever since the collapse—doing their absolute best to pull people out,” the eyewitness said.The person said several students had suffered serious injuries and described the rescue operation as difficult.“Many students have suffered severe injuries. Rescuers are pulling them out with great difficulty,” the eyewitness said.Police teams also reached the site and cordoned off the area as emergency personnel began searching through the debris. Locals and eyewitnesses joined the rescue efforts, using their hands and whatever equipment was available to look for people trapped underneath.The Delhi Fire Service said some people had been rescued from the rubble and taken to nearby hospitals for treatment. articles.title: Devizes family keeping their dog's memory alive with Harvey Rocks
articles.summary: Harvey Rocks - created by the Simpkins family in Wiltshire - are being hidden around the world.
articles.body:
A grieving family's creative project to keep the memory of their beloved dog alive is going global.

The Simpkins family, from Devizes in Wiltshire, lost their 13-year-old Australian Kelpie, Harvey, in August. To cope with their grief, they started painting rocks and hiding them in the town and surrounding areas for people to find.

Anybody who finds a rock is asked to post it on Harvey Rocks Facebook page, before hiding it again for somebody else. Some of the rocks found in Devizes have been taken to Spain and the United States.

Katie Simpkins said: "It's given us a way to talk about Harvey in a positive way and to distract away from the sadness a bit. It keeps his memory alive in a happy way."

Since the family started the project about three weeks ago, they have painted more than 60 rocks.

Boy's parkrun feat inspired by ambulance training

In pictures: River football and rescued cygnets

Trampolinist, 92, among community award winners

Katie said the family-of-four had always been creative, but they all struggled to do anything following Harvey's death.

But after they found a painted rock near their local library, the idea of Harvey's Rocks was born.

The rocks feature various designs including animals, objects and rubber ducks - which Harvey was particularly fond of.

Tris, Katie's husband, said: "We wanted to do something to help us remember Harvey.

"He was one of those very much larger than life character dogs.

"We're collecting rocks, painting them and literally now every evening when the kids are in bed we will sit down and paint rocks instead of going on our phones and watching TV," he added.

The family has hidden rocks in Devizes, Chippenham, Melksham and Trowbridge.

A rock is also set to be left at the summit of Yr Wyddfa, also known as Snowdon, which the family climbed years ago in heavy snow with Harvey.

The family said they hope to continue the idea for as long as possible so Harvey's Rocks can travel "as far across the planet as possible".

articles.title: Indian-American judge extends block on Trump’s mail-voting curbs ahead of midterm polls
articles.summary: US News: A US federal judge has extended a block on President Donald Trump’s executive order seeking sweeping restrictions on mail-in voting, marking another l.
articles.body: A US federal judge has extended a block on President Donald Trump’s executive order seeking sweeping restrictions on mail-in voting, marking another legal setback to the administration less than two months before the November midterm elections.District Judge Indira Talwani, an Indian-American jurist, issued a preliminary injunction on Friday preventing the US Postal Service (USPS) from implementing the new mail-voting procedures.The ruling came as North Carolina began sending mail-in ballots to voters for the November 3 elections.Judge warns of ‘significant disenfranchisement’Talwani, who had earlier temporarily halted the order, said states did not have enough time to overhaul their election systems before ballots were due to be mailed.The judge noted that states were legally required to send millions of ballots within prescribed timelines and could not make major changes this late in the election cycle without risking the disenfranchisement of eligible voters.The latest ruling follows a lawsuit filed by a coalition of 24 state attorneys general challenging Trump’s voting order.What Trump’s mail-voting order seeksTrump signed the executive order in March calling for a nationwide system to verify eligible voters who receive mail-in ballots.Under the proposed system, the USPS would work with states to compile lists of eligible mail voters and deliver ballots only to people included on those lists.The administration has argued that tighter controls are needed to protect elections from fraud. However, critics and voting-rights groups have challenged the president’s authority to impose the changes.No state has so far announced plans to voluntarily adopt the new system.Trump administration expected to appealThe administration had already challenged Talwani’s earlier ruling before the US Supreme Court and is expected to appeal Friday’s injunction as well.The Supreme Court had overturned Talwani’s previous block last month, but the conservative majority did not rule on whether Trump’s executive order itself was lawful.Instead, it found that the legal challenge was brought before the USPS formally issued rules explaining how it would implement the order.After the USPS issued its rule, the states and voting-rights groups renewed their legal challenge, bringing the matter back before Talwani.USPS warns of implementation problemsThe postal service has also raised concerns about whether it has the technology needed to implement the administration’s plan.A USPS whistleblower warned earlier this week of potentially serious problems, saying the systems being prepared to administer the new procedures had been developed in a rushed manner and could result in millions of voters not receiving their mail-in ballots.California Attorney General Rob Bonta, who co-led the state coalition challenging the order, welcomed Talwani’s ruling, saying it would keep the proposed USPS changes blocked while the case proceeds.Mail voting becomes election flashpointTrump has repeatedly criticised mail-in voting and has claimed, without evidence, that the system is vulnerable to widespread fraud. He has also linked mail voting to his false claims that the 2020 presidential election was stolen from him.Despite his criticism, Trump has used mail-in voting himself, including during a Republican primary in Florida.The legal battle comes as Republicans seek to retain their narrow control of Congress in the November midterm elections.Democrats have indicated that winning control of Congress could allow them to block Trump’s agenda and potentially pursue impeachment proceedings.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Palestinians in Gaza bury remains of 100 people recovered from rubble
articles.summary: The remains of thousands more people are believed to be buried under destroyed and damaged buildings in Gaza.
articles.body:
Palestinians in northern Gaza are holding funeral ceremonies for about 100 people, including 60 children, whose remains were recovered from the rubble of destroyed buildings in Gaza City’s Zeitoun neighbourhood.

The remains were carried on Sunday by family members from Zeitoun to al-Ma’madani cemetery in central Gaza City for burial, according to Al Jazeera’s correspondent at the scene, Ghazi al-Aloul.

Civil defence crews and family members had spent weeks digging through the ruins of homes hit during Israel’s genocidal war against Palestinians in Gaza, which began in October 2023.

Many of the victims were part of the extended Malaka family, which alone lost 55 members.

Al-Aloul said families had waited a long time to be able to bury their loved ones in “known, proper cemeteries”. He said that the chance to bury the remains of family members was “not available to every family”, noting that Israeli forces had destroyed and dug up cemeteries elsewhere in Gaza during the war.

Al-Aloul said the remains, though wrapped in shrouds resembling intact bodies, were often only fragments.

“These are bone remains and remnants of belongings that may have been found on the bodies, especially the children’s,” he said, adding that no complete bodies had been recovered from the site because “the Israeli occupation has prolonged this process, and continues to prolong it and prevent it from being completed quickly”.

Raed al-Dahshan, head of Gaza’s civil defence service, told Al Jazeera his teams had formulated plans to carry out recovery operations for thousands more missing bodies, but said the work was being held back by a shortage of heavy machinery.

“We don’t have equipment, we don’t have protective equipment” for rescue workers, he told Al Jazeera.

Dahshan said the recovery of an estimated 8,000 bodies still believed to be under rubble could be completed in about 90 days with proper equipment, but “if that equipment is barred from entering Gaza … this work will continue for years”.

He said his agency had submitted a detailed list of needed equipment to international institutions and was willing to have that machinery remain under international control rather than with the civil defence directly.

He said crews needed large excavators, personal protective equipment and search equipment to locate remains urgently.

On identifying remains, he said crews rely on survivors and neighbouring families to establish who was in a building and where they were at the time of the strike, supported by a team of engineers who sort and document findings in the field. He said Israeli forces’ failure to warn residents before strikes meant “dozens, even hundreds” of homes still required excavation.

Ajith Sunghay, head of the UN human rights office in the occupied Palestinian territories, told Al Jazeera that the scenes were a reminder of “the brutality of this conflict”, noting some of the remains dated back to November 2023.

“Thousands of people are still languishing under this rubble … We’re talking about areas that may be under Israeli military control, 70 percent of Gaza – there’s difficulty accessing these areas to extract these bodies.”

“Accountability must happen … It’s essential that we preserve the evidence we’ve been able to obtain during this sensitive period.”

Gaza’s Health Ministry says at least 73,651 Palestinians have been killed and 174,592 wounded since October 2023.

Similar recovery operations in recent weeks have retrieved more than 100 bodies of people from the Abu Shariah and Hassaniya families who were killed in a single strike, as well as more than 500 bodies from the Al-Taj tower site, officials and activists said.

articles.title: US, Iran engaged in tanker war: Where is the months-long conflict headed?
articles.summary: The US and Iran attack tankers in Strait of Hormuz, as the two sides try to exert control over the strategic waterway.
articles.body:
The United States and Iran have escalated tit-for-tat attacks in the past 24 hours, with Washington targeting three Iranian oil tankers and Tehran hitting tankers and firing a ballistic missile towards US warships patrolling near the Strait of Hormuz.

Experts have dubbed Iran’s targeting of the two US aircraft carriers a “calculated escalation”, as the months-long fighting is increasingly playing out at sea, with both sides trying to exert control over the strategic strait – a global chokepoint used by Tehran as leverage in the war.

The attacks on tankers come as the US claims that an increasing volume of oil has started to flow through the strait, though the exact figures are still debatable, while the naval blockade of Iranian ports continues.

The latest exchanges further dim hopes for a de-escalation through diplomacy as the US-Israel war on Iran has disrupted energy supplies and slowed economic growth around the world.

So, what do we know about the latest tanker wars, and where is the conflict headed?

What do we know about the latest attacks on tankers?

US Central Command (CENTCOM) said its forces struck three Iranian vessels, including a tanker off Kharg Island, the hub through which Iran exported 90 percent of its crude before the war.

Another tanker was struck near Jask, and an unladen vessel was hit in the Gulf of Oman after its crew was told to abandon ship.

CENTCOM said the attacks followed Iranian ballistic missile launches against a US aircraft carrier and navy destroyer, which it said successfully evaded the strikes. No US personnel were injured.

“If you shoot at two of our ships, we will impose an even higher economic cost — taking out three of yours,” CENTCOM commander Admiral Brad Cooper said.

Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said it launched “several ballistic missiles” at the aircraft carrier and destroyer, accusing them of “harassing Iranian ships” and taking part in a naval blockade.

“The Iranians did not only target two ordinary warships – they targeted a missile destroyer and, remarkably, an aircraft carrier … the backbone of the American campaign against Iran,” defence analyst Wolfgang Pusztai told Al Jazeera.

“This is a very, very significant development, and it doesn’t come as a surprise that the Americans retaliated.”

Iran then said its forces also targeted three oil tankers travelling through what it called an “unauthorised route” in the Strait of Hormuz and three US-linked vessels elsewhere.

In a statement carried by Iranian broadcaster IRIB, the IRGC navy warned all vessels in the Gulf or near the Strait of Hormuz not to be “deceived” by the US military and to “refrain from any suspicious movement aimed at transiting unauthorised waterways”.

“Otherwise, you will be targeted,” it said.

On Sunday, Iran claimed it struck an unmanned US vessel trying to enter the Strait of Hormuz, according to The Associated Press news agency.

Washington claimed the Iranian tankers it struck were part of a multibillion-dollar shadow network financing the IRGC and its regional allies.

Iran has long relied partly on a shadow fleet to circumvent sanctions and sell oil, a source of revenue that has become more important since the US began blockading Iranian ports in April.

Iran effectively shut the Strait of Hormuz, through which 20 percent of the world’s oil supplies flowed, in retaliation for the US-Israeli attacks that began on February 28. Some 20 million barrels of oil flowed daily before the war began.

Hassan Ghashghavi, a lawmaker and spokesman for the Iranian Parliament’s National Security Commission, said the attacks on US warships were part of “an existential war with America”, arguing that Washington’s naval blockade “should never have existed” in the first place.

“Naturally, they have acted militarily in violation of all international laws,” he told Al Jazeera, adding that “because America is far from us, it does not see this war as existential”.

Meanwhile, the US has continued to build pressure on Iran to open the key waterway, both militarily and economically.

Last month, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced a raft of economic measures to target Tehran’s financial interests across the world.

Bessent said the US would target all of Iran’s sources of revenue, including oil, to prevent other countries and companies from doing business with Tehran.

This comes despite US assertions of normalcy in the Strait of Hormuz, with Washington insisting the waterway is open and that dozens of ships carrying millions of barrels of oil transit it each day.

Last week, Bessent claimed that some 17 million barrels of crude oil a day had been shipped out recently, according to a report in the United Kingdom’s The Times newspaper. Al Jazeera, however, could not independently verify the claims in the report.

President Donald Trump claimed last month that the US was in “total control” of the strait.

Yet figures from marine analytics firm Kpler show only six vessels crossed the strait on Wednesday, 11 on Tuesday and five on Monday, with a 10-day average of just 13 vessels per day.

The attacks are adding to concerns about global energy supplies.

Brent crude futures closed on Friday at $96.28 a barrel, their highest level since July 24, up from roughly $70 before the war.

Predictably, US oil and gas prices have also skyrocketed, coming at a crucial time for Trump as Americans head to the polls for midterm elections in November.

Diesel hit a new record price in the US on Friday, soaring to an average of $5.85 a gallon ($1.55 per litre) for the first time ever. Polls have repeatedly suggested a majority of Americans oppose the war, which has also plunged Trump’s popularity.

A Reuters/Ipsos survey conducted in late August found that only 31 percent of Americans back the war, while 63 percent are against it.

The same polling suggested Trump’s approval rating has dropped to 33 percent, down from 40 percent since the fighting began.

The renewed exchanges of strikes between Iran and the US mark an escalation in the six-month-long conflict, according to the director of the Middle East studies programme at George Washington University, Sina Azodi.

Azodi told Al Jazeera that neither side will “cave in” because it “will not look good on them, so the only option is to escalate”.

He said unless there is a political settlement, the war will continue.

“There’s going to be more clashes between the Iranians and the Americans. There can be miscalculations. There can be more civilian casualties”, especially on the Iranian side, Azodi said.

“The [US] secretary of defence can send more troops to the region, but I don’t think the Iranians are going to back down. They’re going to resist that blockade and impose further costs on the United States.”

He said the goal of the US and Iran is to force the other to back down. “The winner is going to be the one that can accept more costs and punishment,” Azodi said.

Commenting on Iran’s strategy, Ali Akbar Dareini, an analyst at the Center for Strategic Studies in Tehran, echoed Azodi, saying the US attacks on Iranian oil tankers are a “big issue” that Iran cannot afford to let “go unanswered”.

“Does it make Iran surrender? No, it compels Iran. It incentivises Iran to lash out and retaliate” more harshly, Dareini told Al Jazeera.

He said the US naval blockade, coupled with sanctions, is inflicting severe pain on Iran, but added the latter has plans to counter it. Iran cannot tolerate this naval blockade to continue, so Iran is already making preparations to break the siege.

“At the same time, Iran definitely has its own plans to make sure that oil prices will shoot up over $100 per barrel,” Dareini said.
